text:
Five European Union countries are pushing ahead with plans to start deporting asylum seekers whose applications are rejected to third countries outside the bloc, potentially in Africa, after the EU approved new rules this week that clear the way for the practice.

Greece, Germany, Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands have agreed on a common framework to establish "return hubs" outside the EU to which people who have exhausted their legal options to remain in Europe could be transferred if they cannot be sent back to their own countries of origin.

"When it comes to return hubs, it's progressing very well," Danish Interior Minister Morten Bødskov told reporters Thursday, according to AFP. "We are moving in the right direction."

He previously said Denmark expected "to be ready to transfer the first irregular migrants to a partner country outside the EU within 2027."

Greek Migration Minister Thanos Plevris told Politico that Greece expects to have a pilot project in place in the first half of next year.

No potential destinations for EU return hubs have been confirmed, although Rwanda has been reported as a possible partner in the project. A Greek government statement on the plans said the hubs would be established in safe third countries, "particularly on the African continent."

The EU itself has presented the idea of return hubs as a potential deterrent to irregular immigration. A discussion paper published by the EU's governing European Council in October 2025 said the hubs could "incentivize voluntary returns," because migrants who fail to comply with a deportation order could face transfer to a hub instead.

It said the policy could also discourage people without a valid asylum claim from making dangerous journeys to Europe.

The rules adopted this week by the EU establish a bloc-wide legal framework for returns and allow member states to conclude bilateral or unilateral agreements with countries outside the bloc, but with stipulations.

Under the rules, "any such agreement or arrangement may only be concluded with a non-EU country that respects international human rights standards and principles of international law, including the principle of non-refoulement," which guarantees that no individual can be sent back to a country where they would face torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, punishment or other irreparable harm.

EU follows U.S. and U.K. examples

The Trump administration has enthusiastically embraced the use of third-country deportations to remove undocumented migrants from the United States. More than 100 deportees were sent to eight African countries over a 10-day period in August, according to internal U.S. government documents obtained by CBS News.

The deportees were sent to destinations including the African nations of Liberia, Rwanda, Eswatini and Sierra Leone.

Plevris, Greece's migration minister, has praised the Trump administration's approach.

"I am a fan of President Trump," he told Breitbart in August. "But if you ask me what was the best thing he did, it was change the migration policy of the USA, because now we have a new migration policy also in Europe."

Other European governments have experimented with deportations to third nations before, however, with mixed results.

"No shortcut around the difficult parts of migration policy"

Britain's former Conservative Party government sought to send asylum seekers who arrived through irregular routes to Rwanda to have their claims processed there. The U.K. Supreme Court ruled the scheme unlawful in 2023, before it ever got going, over the risk that refugees could ultimately be returned to countries where they faced persecution.

The following year, the policy was formally abandoned by the new Labour Party government after the Conservatives were voted out of power. The British Home Office said £715 million (almost $950 million) had been spent on the Rwanda program by June 2024, and no asylum seekers were forcibly relocated. Four people traveled voluntarily to Rwanda under the program.

"One lesson may be that European governments should expect litigation, even where the third country looks considerably less controversial than Rwanda," Peter Walsh, a senior researcher at the University of Oxford's Migration Observatory, told CBS News on Friday.

"These policies are often justified as deterrence measures, and that assumes a sufficiently large share of people believe there is a realistic chance they will actually be transferred," Walsh said. "If only a very small proportion can be moved, the deterrent may be much less credible."

"The broader lesson from Rwanda is that externalization is not a shortcut around the difficult parts of migration policy," he said. "It may relocate some of those difficulties geographically, but governments still have to deal with courts, individual rights, administrative capacity, countries that may not cooperate with returns, and substantial costs"

The push for return hubs is part of a broader effort by European nations to tighten their immigration policies amid intense pressure on governments to increase the number of people without a legal right to remain who are actually removed.

Jacob Reynolds, policy director at the Freedom and Sovereignty Initiative Europe, a right-wing think tank based in Brussels, called the EU decision to embrace these hubs a "welcome step towards gaining control of our borders and removing those who have no right to be here."

But he added that "outsourcing the problem of illegal migration to third countries — as the EU has long done — risks avoiding the broader problem: the lack of control over EU countries' borders."

He called for "much more fundamental action" to address "the generous regimes available to asylum seekers in Europe," and said until that happened, "the problem will not be solved."

text:
Republicans are struggling with how to thread the needle on immigration ahead of what is expected to be a bruising midterm season in which many voters have soured on the Trump administration’s aggressive enforcement.

But the party has spent two years championing policies that resulted from President Trump running on “securing” the border, including a pledge to carry out the largest mass deportation operation in history.

Two back-to-back statements from Sen. Jim Justice (R-W.Va.) illustrate the problem.

In an interview with Politico on Tuesday, the lawmaker said immigration officers have been “dragging people away that have lived on your street corner for 15 years.”

“I don’t know that we need to be doing that stuff,” he told the outlet.

“To get better, the first thing you got to do is admit you’re doing something wrong,” he added, nodding to the need to “step back.”

But the next day, he walked the comments back.

“Let me be crystal clear: I support President Trump’s immigration strategy, full stop,” he wrote on the social platform X.

Trump has also acknowledged the issue.

“Frankly, it’s the hardest job that I’ve had,” Trump said during a Hispanic Heritage Month event at the White House on Wednesday. “They’ll say you’re too tough or you’re too soft. Get tougher, get softer. No matter what you do, it’s always tough.”

The president’s comments come as a Thursday AP-NORC poll found Trump had a 39 percent approval rating on immigration, while recent Politico polling found divides in how the GOP rated Trump on the issue. Thirty-one percent of those polled who did not identify as MAGA said Trump’s deportation campaign is too aggressive.

Republicans are also struggling with the Hispanic voting bloc, which boosted Trump and the GOP in 2024. Signs of disapproval among Hispanic and Latino voters are particularly noticeable in Texas and Florida, as the GOP looks to keep control of Congress in November.

Twenty percent of Hispanic voters in Florida who supported Trump in 2024 said they would not repeat their vote, according to a UnidosUS survey from this spring. Meanwhile, a September Cook Political Report and TelevisaUnivision poll found that 18 percent of Texan Latinos who voted for Trump said they no longer back him.

Several conservative voices have grumbled about impacts.

Paul LePage, a former Republican governor of Maine who is now running for Congress, has bragged about being “Donald Trump before Donald Trump became popular.” But he revealed recently that his son’s father-in-law, who he has said was living in the U.S. legally, was “being deported because he came from a country that’s not liked by certain people in Washington. That’s not right.”

LePage, however, has largely refused to answer additional questions after his comments garnered headlines, saying earlier this week it was a “personal matter.”

In Florida, Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R) saw that her district, which has one of the largest foreign-born populations of any in the country, was so disenchanted with Trump’s immigration policies that she campaigned on it.

“Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” Salazar said in a September ad. In the ad, she stands in front of the White House, addressing Trump.

She faced some pushback for her comments, including from constituents and Trump himself, who criticized the congresswoman in a dozen social media posts after the ad aired. Border czar Tom Homan also dismissed Salazar’s take.

“Give me an example where we went too far. That’s a pretty bold statement to make,” Homan told CBS News in a recent interview.

Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall (R), also a vocal proponent of Trump’s immigration policies, offered tepid criticism after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers conducted enforcement operations in his home state, saying they did not sufficiently coordinate with police.

“Law enforcement officers were not given advance notice or the level of cooperation we would expect from ICE’s enforcement and removal operations. As a result, there have been mass disruptions to local communities and businesses,” he said in a statement late last month.

ICE has made changes to shift the optics around their immigration enforcement, moving away from aggressive raids that were advertised in advance on social media.

But many of the tactics remain the same. ICE officers are operating in unmarked cars and donning plainclothes — details that have prompted some migrants to flee amid confusion.

Arrests, however, are still ticking up and are increasingly likely to be carried out against those who have no criminal record and who even have immigration petitions in processing.

ICE arrested about 50,000 migrants in both July and August — record-breaking figures.

Meanwhile, internal Justice Department data obtained by The Hill shows cases handled by the Office of Immigration Litigation have soared, with cases jumping from roughly 7,700 to nearly 9,500 since the start of Trump’s second term. Many of those are habeas petitions from the nearly 70,000 people currently held in immigration detention.

Other Republican senators said they’re hearing less from constituents about ICE now that the operations are quieter.

“Generally speaking, people want to see folks that commit violent crimes and, you know, removed from that aren’t supposed to be here, under deportation, be … taken out of the country,” said Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.). “There’s been scrutiny on methods, and certain incidences have had some very sad results, obviously, with a couple deaths.”

“I feel like it’s calmed down in terms of what ICE is doing, and they’ve upped their training.”

Sen. James Lankford (R-Okla.) said he had also heard fewer concerns about ICE, although the Oklahoma Cattlemen’s Association joined trade groups in Kansas and Texas in a letter last week describing the disruption recent raids have had on the industry.

Lankford said the complaints that come to him are “fewer than I used to hear about that.”

“But yes, I mean, we’ve always heard that.”

Democrats, however, believe Republicans will suffer on Election Day given the unpopularity of Trump’s immigration enforcement and deportations after several fatal shootings this year.

“They’re no longer going after ‘the worst of the worst’ — they are acting like the worst of the worst,” Rep. Jamie Raskin (Md.), the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, said during a recent hearing on Trump immigration efforts.

“Trump’s poll numbers have sunk like a stone, and the majority of Americans have rejected their authoritarian police-state tactics.”

Rep. Pramila Jayapal (Wash.), the top Democrat on the House Judiciary subcommittee on immigration, said the Trump administration’s focus on meeting arrest quotas has backfired.

“They are continuing this strategy quietly now because it was unpopular when it was loud,” she told The Hill last month after the release of record-setting arrest figures.

“But they’re going to find out in November that it’s unpopular when it’s quiet as well.”

title: Five Great Reads: ICE 2.0, millennial motherhood, and skinny-dipping with Christine Baranski
description:
Grab a coffee and dig in, digest, and reflect on harrowing accounts of Trump’s immigration crackdown, investigations into modern motherhood and masculinity, and for a bit of weekend fun, we leave you with some celebrity gossip.
Inside Trump’s new immigration dragnet At the peak of Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, armoured vehicles occupied neighbourhoods, while masked agents violently pulled people from the streets.
In this series, ICE 2.0, Guardian reporters track how, despite the administration’s change of tactics, ICE is everywhere.

text:
Hello and welcome to the weekend.

The Guardian’s range was on display this week across these five very different stories. Grab a coffee and dig in, digest, and reflect on harrowing accounts of Trump’s immigration crackdown, investigations into modern motherhood and masculinity, and for a bit of weekend fun, we leave you with some celebrity gossip.

Enjoy.

1. Inside Trump’s new immigration dragnet

At the peak of Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, armoured vehicles occupied neighbourhoods, while masked agents violently pulled people from the streets. After officers killed two US citizens during the raids in Minneapolis, public backlash prompted Trump to try a new approach. Now, ICE arrests have hit record levels. In this series, ICE 2.0, Guardian reporters track how, despite the administration’s change of tactics, ICE is everywhere.

Notable quote: “Before, they were storming around, making a lot of noise Now, they are moving more quietly.”

The violence continues: People are arrested while pumping gas, leaving behind their empty cars. They are arrested on their way to work, or on their way home. Recently, an ICE agent shot Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez in Texas. That same day, in Grand Rapids, Michigan, a Guatemalan man died in a fiery crash while fleeing federal immigration agents. ICE is now detaining more immigrants than ever before, despite the new secretary of homeland security, Markwayne Mullin, promising to avoid negative headlines by cutting the flash and fanfare.

How long will it take to read: Under four minutes.

Further reading: All the stories from the series ICE 2.0: inside Trump’s new immigration dragnet.

2. Why does millennial motherhood feel so impossible?

Women today are more educated, more employed and more engaged in childcare arrangements than ever before. But research shows that the expectations facing modern mothers continue to grow. In Australia, the statistics illuminate a global phenomenon. New research shows that the cost for Australian families of raising two or more children has risen to at least $36,500 a year. The cost of keeping a family afloat has increased by 134% in two decades, while household income has grown by only 102% in the same period.

Between juggling rising costs and managing careers, is there any way out of the total overwhelm?

A problem with no solution: In this personal piece, Kate Lyons writes that millennial women no longer feel trapped in their homes like generations before, but rather, by the impossible juggle of managing their career, relationships and children. Lyons recounts a friend reaching out for advice late one night after their five-year-old had a meltdown before bed. Another woman Lyons spoke to got so desperate she turned towards ChatGPT, asking the AI chatbot how to make her life work. But solutions are not easy to come by. After Lyons assessed the state of her living room, which, “looks as though someone has taken the contents of a laundry basket, a toy box and a nappy bag and Jackson Pollocked the floor with them”, all she could offer was solidarity.

Notable quote: “It’s not that I want to be at home five days a week. I don’t want to be exactly like my mum was. But I want to pick them up from school and take them home and calmly wind down the day with them. There’s absolutely no way I can do that.”

How long will it take to read: Just under six minutes.

Further reading: Why birthrates are plummeting, and why workplaces were built for men.

3. Trump’s testosterone culture war

Polls show that Donald Trump is losing support with the bros that got him elected. As the midterms approach, the cost of living and the war on Iran have left male voters increasingly disillusioned. So how does one win them back? The health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, and the defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, seem to think the hormone testosterone, often known simply as “T”, is the answer. Or as Sam Wolfson explains, Trump is hoping that “the male populace will vote not with their heads or their hearts, but with their hogs”.

The testosterone dog-whistle: Testosterone is found in the bodies of men and women, with a low amount all that is needed for normal function. But the hormone has emerged on the frontlines of the Trump administration’s many culture wars. While the war in Iran causes problems for Trump back home, Hegseth has shifted the military message to one of machismo. On the campaign trail, he said, “We’re reminding our warriors that their sole purpose is to be the most lethal fighting force on the planet. Full stop. We’re not here to do social engineering, or social justice, or gender-bending, or DEI, or dudes and dresses.” But Wolfson writes that Hegseth’s testosterone push is a “sciencey” way to dog-whistle his sexist message.

Notable quote: “Everything has been politicized in the United States. Vaccines are liberal and TRT is Maga. The needle is apolitical but the content of the syringe is decided by who you vote for.”

How long will it take to read: eight minutes.

Further reading: The Pentagon and “incel” slang, plus RFK Jr’s “peptide wild west”.

4. Exposing the world’s biggest porn bosses

Patricia Nilsson was determined to bring porn industry leaders out of the shadows. For five years, she subjected the adult industry to forensic analysis in an effort to reveal who was getting rich through porn and how they were doing it. For decades, the owners of these companies have escaped scrutiny, and they have often enjoyed relative anonymity. But porn is everywhere, and for many young men and women, adult content can be their default sex education. Nilsson argues the owners of businesses that are recalibrating our sexual culture deserve further investigation.

Notable quote: “My argument is not that we should be neutral towards porn, but that we need to accept and understand it as a real industry, and ask what its growth and popularity says about the state of our economy and the world of work.”

The story of porn is the story of the internet: Nilsson argues that even if you do not consume explicit content online, the industry has shaped the way you interact with the digital world. We have porn to thank, she says, for high-quality video streaming and the way influencers sell their online personas. “Staring at content that is algorithmically engineered to arouse you is a perfect metaphor for our relationship with our devices and the internet and social media,” Nilsson says.

How long will it take to read: About five minutes.

Further reading: The malignant rise of OnlyFans managers and the rise of deepfake pornography in schools.

5. Christine Baranski and Richard E Grant on sex scenes, parties and theatre

Christine Baranski and Richard E Grant have stories to tell. The actors have joined forces for the first time in a London production of Noël Coward’s comedic play Hay Fever. The Guardian sat down with the actors to get a glimpse of the tall tales told backstage.

Notable quote: When asked if she has ever worked with Grant before, Baranski wryly says: “Regrettably not. We could have had some good fun a few decades ago. A girl could have got into some real trouble. But here we are, and now we’re the veterans.”

Skinny dipping in the dark: Recalling her “marvellous house” on a lake in Connecticut, Baranski recounts an evening spent with Mark Rylance when the pair went skinny-dipping and ended up howling at the moon till four in the morning. Pressed on whether taking your clothes off is a prerequisite for visiting, Baranski says: “I encourage people only if they’re comfortable and if it’s pitch dark.”

How long will it take to read: five minutes of gossipy joy.

Further reading: How Richard E Grant ended up on Celebrity Traitors.

Department of Homeland Security agents compiled extensive dossiers on people observing Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations in the field, then stored them in a system called the Investigative Case Management (ICM) designed and managed by Palantir Technologies, according to Wired.

The magazine’s report on Friday stems from a proposed class action lawsuit fthat our observers have brought to state courts in Maine; the case was put under seal in September and a redacted version released Friday, according to Wired. JoAnna Suriani, an attorney for Protect Democracy representing the plaintiffs, told Wired, “The government is treating people who exercise their First Amendment rights and seek to hold it accountable as criminal suspects, and that’s what we’re asking the court to stop.”

A DHS spokesperson told Wired the claim is “meritless” and “the underlying lawsuit is based on the lie that there is a database of ‘domestic terrorists’ run by DHS.” (It’s noteworthy that #1 DHS booster President Donald Trump has made it very clear he wants to do exactly that.) ICE is part of DHS, whose other subordinate agencies include Homeland Security Investigations and Customs and Border Protection. Palantir, of course, is right-wing Silicon Valley billionaire Peter Thiel’s notorious data firm explicitly named after an all-seeing orb in The Lord of the Rings that a godlike being of pure evil, Sauron, uses to spy on enemies and gaslight elves.

ICE agents shot and killed a 25-year-old father named Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine in July during a summer surge in ICE operations that drew nationwide outrage. Immigration authorities have shot at least 21 people during Trump’s second term, resulting in at least 10-11 deaths. Allegations in the lawsuit include that DHS agents drove by protesters and observers’ homes to intimidate them, and that a DHS agent identified in the lawsuit as “Agent J.C” created ICM profiles on six of them. (The government’s count is actually eight, Wired noted.) J.C. allegedly tagged two people filmed in a parking lot in the ICM database as “Threat to Law Enforcement, Professional Protestor.” (Paid protesters, let alone “professional” protesters, basically do not exist beyond the kind of astroturfing campaigns sometimes run by lobbyists, corporations, or politicians.)

The suit also alleges J.C. sent the photos of the two individuals to a CBP officer for face recognition in an app called Mobile Query, as well as ran one of the plaintiff’s license plates through a LexisNexis database (Accurint) after that individual photographed an arrest in Portland, Maine. The suit states J.C. then called the plaintiff’s spouse, who is also a plaintiff, and threatened them that individuals who “do anything like that in the future… might get added to a domestic terrorism watchlist.”

The Palantir-built ICM is used by HSI to track case files and has won nearly $126 million in government contracts to maintain and expand it since 2022 alone, according to Wired, including $30 million to develop “ImmigrationOS.”

An aide to a state assembly member from San Francisco has been released by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, 15 days after he was detained at a Las Vegas airport, her office said Friday.

Ho Yin Mo, a field representative in Assemblymember Catherine Stefani's San Francisco office, was granted bond by an immigration judge Wednesday and was released from ICE custody Friday, Stefani's office said in a press release.

Mo, a former TV news reporter originally from Hong Kong, was taken into custody by ICE on Sept. 17 at Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas during a "targeted enforcement operation," ICE said at the time.

ICE said that Mo lawfully entered the U.S. in January 2020 on a temporary basis, but "illegally overstayed his welcome" by not leaving the country by May of that year.

PREVIOUS REPORT: San Francisco assemblymember's aide, former Bay Area news reporter detained by ICE, officials say

Mo has worked for the Democratic assemblymember since January 2025. He previously worked at KTSF, the largest Asian-language broadcast station in the U.S.

"Mo's release confirms what we knew all along: He is a lawful public servant and a cherished part of our Bay Area family, and he should never have been detained," Stefani said in the statement.

Stefani's office said Mo will probably continue to face the threat of deportation by the Trump Administration.

"I'm overwhelmed with gratitude for the tireless work of Assemblymember Stefani, my legal counsel and every individual who advocated on my behalf," Mo said in the statement. "I'm excited to return to my work serving San Franciscans, who have shown time and again what community truly means."

Mo assists Cantonese- and Mandarin-speaking people in Stefani's office and interprets at meetings with her. He helps constituents navigate state agencies and access disability benefits, affordable health care coverage, childcare and food support, the office said.

description:
Harris County has the second-largest Salvadoran population in the country, with over 110,000 Salvadorans, behind only Los Angeles County.
Her journey to Texas The gang violence that surged in El Salvador in the late 1990s had already driven her two siblings out.
How El Salvador got TPS By the time Claudia arrived in Houston in 2001, generations of Central American immigrants had already put down roots.
A decade later, after two devastating earthquakes struck the country in 2001, the U.S. gave El Salvador TPS status again, which has spanned nearly all of Claudia’s adult life.
Stay in the country, or leave for El Salvador.
text:
Most mornings, Claudia gets up at 5 a.m., tying on a black apron and wrapping pupusas in aluminum foil for her daughters’ lunch. But on the morning of Sept. 9, she was still in bed.

She was frantically refreshing the news on her phone. Then, she stopped on one video announcing the cancellation of Temporary Protected Status, a humanitarian program that allowed her and thousands of other Salvadorans to temporarily live and work in the U.S.

A few minutes into the video, an attorney explained it in simple terms: The program had expired, but there was no official termination date yet.

Her three daughters climbed into bed beside her as she listened. “Did they cancel it or not?” she remembered thinking.

For Claudia and others protected under the program, the decision can determine whether they can remain in the U.S. or have to return to their home countries, where violence and instability continue.

She told her daughters what she heard, and they began to cry.

“ No mami, y ahora qué vamos a hacer?” they asked. “What is going to happen to us?”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Her oldest daughter, 15, had spent years getting ahead in school and started earning college credits this year. But that morning she told her mom the credits didn’t matter if they meant being separated from her.

But Claudia could only offer them the same words that she’s carried over the last 25 years, words inspired by her own mom: “We have to keep going.”

WIDE NET: This Bellaire family voted for Trump. Now his immigration crackdown could separate them.

She is one of 170,000 Salvadorans whose futures remain uncertain as they wait for the Trump administration to decide whether to renew or end TPS, which allows people from countries facing war, natural disasters, or other extraordinary conditions to temporarily remain and work in the U.S. The program was set to expire for El Salvador on Sept. 9, but the Department of Homeland Security said recipients would remain protected while an announcement was pending — leaving families like Claudia’s in limbo.

The Houston Chronicle is identifying Claudia by her first name because of the uncertainty around TPS and fears of deportation and family separation.

For Houston, the stakes are close to home. Harris County has the second-largest Salvadoran population in the country, with over 110,000 Salvadorans, behind only Los Angeles County. Claudia became part of that community in 2001, though Texas wasn’t in her future plans.

Her journey to Texas

The gang violence that surged in El Salvador in the late 1990s had already driven her two siblings out.

But one encounter convinced her mother that Claudia, then 19, had to leave, too. Claudia pointed to her left cheekbone, then her neck and chest, tracing the places where a gang member had held a machete.

“I wasn’t safe there anymore,” she said in Spanish. “So she made the decision, ‘No, you have to go, even if it means we give you the only thing we have.’”

Her parents took out a loan against their home to complete her journey. Claudia understood what they were risking: if she didn’t pay it back, they could lose the only home they had.

In 2001, she traveled north with a cousin and several women from her hometown, the group watching over each other along the way. At one point, Claudia was crammed into the storage compartment at the bottom of a bus, near the tires. Several hours passed and when she finally climbed out, her legs buckled, and a man had to help her up.

Her journey took her to Arizona, California and eventually Houston. She remembers studying the roads, cars and signs around her before making her way to her brother’s home. By the next day, she was cleaning houses.

OPINION: America helped drive Salvadorans from home. We can’t expel them again.

How El Salvador got TPS

By the time Claudia arrived in Houston in 2001, generations of Central American immigrants had already put down roots. Neighborhoods such as Gulfton became gathering places for families from El Salvador, Honduras and Guatemala, while organizations like CRECEN grew out of an earlier wave of migration during armed conflicts in Central America.

Congress created TPS through the Immigration Act of 1990, and El Salvador was the first country designated under the program as its civil war continued. That initial protection lasted 18 months.

A decade later, after two devastating earthquakes struck the country in 2001, the U.S. gave El Salvador TPS status again, which has spanned nearly all of Claudia’s adult life.

The debate over how long the protection should continue has followed TPS holders for years. In 2017, the Department of Homeland Security had planned to strip TPS from Salvadorans the following year, but litigation blocked that decision and the Biden administration eventually rescinded it in 2023.

Now, the Trump administration is targeting TPS again as it wages its immigration crackdown. Haiti’s designation was scheduled to end Feb. 3, 2026, but a federal court temporarily blocked the decision. After a Supreme Court ruling in June, the termination took effect July 27.

Houston became ‘less temporary’ and more like home

After a few months in Houston and juggling three jobs, Claudia accomplished her mission: she paid her parents’ debt off.

She went from managing her week selling perfume, jewelry and clothes to cleaning homes and working in a restaurant — a job that she has now held for 25 years. Claudia even sent additional money to help rebuild her family’s ideal home and helped them buy a cow, something she had once dreamed about.

Looking back on the work it took to get there, she came to a conclusion: “Valió la pena.” It had been worth it.

Houston is also where she became a mom to her three U.S.-born daughters.

Some mornings she would wake up early to knock on doors, praying for someone she trusted enough to watch over them. One day, the girls stayed with a sitter for as long as 14 hours, so Claudia could pick up an extra shift.

“I had to,” she said. “Because I needed the work to get them ahead.”

One summer, she asked a teacher to enroll her oldest in summer school even though her daughter was one of the top students in her class. Claudia needed somewhere safe for her daughter to go while she was at work.

Her life now revolves around work, school drop-offs, church and her daughters’ activities. She volunteers through her church, including teaching in her prayer group, and has spent about three years involved with CRECEN, making room in her busy schedule for meetings and rallies.

What comes next

Only now, as a mother herself, does Claudia understand the bravery it took for her parents to decide between staying together and separating to keep their three children safe.

It’s that same courage, she says, that she wants to show her own daughters as they navigate this new uncertainty.

Rose Gondiez, an attorney with the Immigrant Legal Resource Center, said part of the issue is the lack of a formal federal decision about what will happen for Salvadorans with TPS.

COMMUNITY PROFILE: Gulfton is the 'Ellis Island of Houston.' Residents say fear of ICE is hurting the neighborhood

“In the absence of an official decision,” Gondiez said, “thousands of families are unclear about decisions about their jobs and their families and their futures,” including whether they can continue to feel safe in the country.

Gondiez said TPS holders should consult with an immigration attorney about whether they might qualify for another form of relief. She also recommends that families begin making preparedness plans rather than waiting until all protections are lost.

“While we're in this limbo period, it's just a good thing to do regardless,” she said. “I would also say they should stay alert to changes in workers' employment authorization.”

Claudia has started preparing at home, organizing her daughters’ passports and other documents alongside a list of family contacts. She’s pushed her 15-year-old to get her driver’s license. “You have to learn how to drive,” Claudia told her. “Maybe you won’t be able to take the house with you, but at least take the car.”

The days leading up to Sept. 9, she spent an evening with her kids and they discussed their options. Stay in the country, or leave for El Salvador.

Claudia has decided that if her protected status does end, she’ll leave on her own rather than face the risk of being deported or worse, detained.

Houston has seen a sharp increase in ICE enforcement this year. Claudia’s neighborhood has seen it, too. She’s heard from multiple neighbors about ICE sightings in places she frequents.

ALSO READ: Houston is becoming a destination for a new wave of Cuban migrants. Here's why.

It’s a fear she holds as she waits for the government’s decision. Despite her own fears, Claudia still drives her daughters to school, goes to work and shows up to protests. Staying home in fear, she said, won’t teach her daughters to stand and fight back.

“I can’t put my fear into them,” she said. “My fear, I keep it inside.”

She has watched her 15-year-old become more passionate about advocating, informing other TPS holders of their rights and protesting at rallies. Her daughter now understands why her mother brings her along, and she has begun to tell Claudia that she wants to defend her.

“I don’t know if I’m always going to be here with you,” Claudia told her. “You have to learn how to stand up for yourselves.”

So, that morning on Sept. 9, Claudia first comforted her girls crying beside her in bed. But a few hours later, the family headed together to a vigil. Her oldest stood beside her two younger sisters, holding blue-lettered signs that spelled out TPS.

text:
The family of Renee Good has filed two federal lawsuits over her fatal shooting by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent in Minneapolis, including a civil rights case against ICE agent Jonathan Ross and senior Trump administration officials that invokes provisions of the Reconstruction-era Ku Klux Klan Act.

The lawsuits, filed October 1, 2026, in the U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota, take separate legal paths. One names the United States as the sole defendant and seeks damages under the Federal Tort Claims Act for Good’s death. The other names Ross and several current and former Trump administration officials, accusing them of participating in or failing to stop a civil rights conspiracy tied to Operation Metro Surge.

Good, a 37-year-old mother of three, was shot by Ross on January 7, 2026, after she and her partner, Becca Good, encountered immigration agents in their south Minneapolis neighborhood. Good was inside her vehicle when another agent ordered her out. She then began moving the vehicle before Ross opened fire.

The civil rights lawsuit invokes 42 U.S.C. §§ 1985 and 1986, Reconstruction-era provisions Congress enacted in 1871 to reach conspiracies that interfere with equal protection and other constitutional rights.

The family is invoking a statute enacted to combat Ku Klux Klan-era civil rights conspiracies, not accusing the defendants of Klan membership. It argues that federal officials participated in or failed to stop a modern conspiracy to interfere with constitutional rights.

The complaint also points to Section 1985’s Reconstruction-era language covering people who go “in disguise on the highway” to deprive others of equal protection, wording Congress adopted in response to Klan violence after the Civil War.

Along with Ross, the case names White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, former Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino, Corey Lewandowski, Tom Homan, former ICE Acting Director Todd Lyons and unidentified federal agents.

The family alleges Good’s shooting grew out of a broader pattern of aggressive enforcement during Operation Metro Surge, including actions directed at people perceived to be Somali or Hispanic and residents who documented or protested immigration operations. The plaintiffs contend that Good’s death was connected to that broader effort rather than an isolated encounter between one officer and one civilian.

Ross is also accused of using excessive force in violation of the Fourth Amendment under the Supreme Court’s 1971 decision in Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents, alongside wrongful death and other claims under Minnesota law.

According to the family, Good and Becca Good had dropped their son off at school before encountering federal agents on Portland Avenue. The lawsuit says Renee Good stopped her vehicle and honked to alert neighbors while Becca Good got out and began recording the officers.

The complaint describes Good as an unarmed civilian who was not the subject of an investigation and says she posed no threat to the agents. As Ross walked near her vehicle while recording on his phone, Good told him, “I’m not mad at you.” Another agent then approached and ordered her out of the vehicle.

Video cited in accounts of the shooting shows Good briefly reverse and then move forward while turning the steering wheel to the right. Ross, positioned near the front-left side of the vehicle, fired into it. Federal officials have defended the shooting as a justified use of force, while the family contends Ross was no longer in the vehicle’s path when he fired.

The second case seeks damages directly from the United States, alleging that Ross and other federal employees committed wrongful acts for which the government can be held liable under the Federal Tort Claims Act. The complaint brings wrongful death claims under Minnesota law based on allegations including battery, assault, false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligence.

Becca Good separately alleges intentional and negligent infliction of emotional distress, saying she was standing nearby when Ross fired into the vehicle and witnessed her partner’s death. The FTCA case will be tried before a judge, while the civil rights lawsuit against the individual defendants demands a jury trial.

The shooting drew national scrutiny as the Trump administration expanded immigration enforcement in Minnesota, with senior officials quickly describing Good’s actions as domestic terrorism. Her family and attorneys dispute that characterization and maintain she was attempting to leave the scene.

Ross has not been criminally charged in the shooting. Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty has continued investigating the deaths of Good and Alex Pretti, another U.S. citizen fatally shot by federal immigration officers in Minneapolis later in January. Local investigators have said they faced difficulties obtaining federal evidence after the Justice Department ended its usual cooperation with local authorities.

The White House has rejected the allegations. A spokesperson said the administration would “vigorously defend” itself against the lawsuits and called the cases baseless.

text:
The Supreme Court returns to the bench Monday to begin its new term after a summer that was anything but quiet. But it’s the cases not yet scheduled that could have the biggest impact.

That’s because of the court’s “shadow docket,” which allows justices to grant emergency orders and rulings, or even add cases to the schedule.

Through that mechanism, the court has already set up a hearing for December on a controversial policy in which people who cannot be deported to their homeland are instead sent to a third country. It’s part of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

The court agreed to take up the case — after a lower court ordered the cancellation of a deportation flight carrying around 70 people.

“I, at this point, see no signs that the Trump administration is going to significantly slow down,” said Loyola Law School professor Jessica Levinson.

At the same time, the court is preparing for the wild card of the midterms this November, which could potentially lead to litigation and emergency appeals.

“Even though we have a piece of the puzzle, we do not have a clear view of what the Supreme Court term looks like,” said Levinson.

Already, the high court has a full docket. Justices will hear arguments Monday about whether states can hold private companies responsible for damage caused by releasing dangerous chemicals into the environment.

“The question really is whether or not there can be actions under state law for greenhouse emissions that lead to climate change or whether or not those types of claims can only be heard under federal law,” Levinson said.

The case has garnered attention, especially after Justice Samuel Alito announced his recusal. He didn’t give a reason, but it came after several left-leaning groups raised concerns about his stock holdings in oil companies.

The court will also hear a case on whether a state can limit AR-15-style semiautomatic weapons, a case on additional requirements for voter registration and a case on parental rights when a runaway child experiencing gender dysphoria is provided shelter.

Although President Donald Trump has benefitted from the conservative 6-3 majority in his second term, it doesn’t mean every decision has gone his way. In several cases the conservative members, including Chief Justice John Roberts, have sided with the three liberal justices.

Some decisions will come down as soon as December, but the bulk of the cases won’t be decided until late next spring.

text:
A judge ruled that a federal law banning noncitizen voting is unconstitutional, dismissing a case against an illegal immigrant who allegedly voted in the 2020 election.

U.S. District Judge David Leibowitz for the Southern District of Florida, a Biden appointee, on Thursday threw out a federal charge of illegal voting against Chelsea Michelle Ann Cox, a Jamaican national who allegedly cast a ballot in the 2020 presidential election, .

Federal prosecutors alleged that Cox knowingly voted in Broward County, Fla., on Oct. 29, 2020, in a misdemeanor charge filed against her last year. Cox allegedly overstayed a tourist visa, using a fake U.S. Virgin Islands birth certificate to obtain identification and register to vote.

Leibowitz wrote in his 31-page that a federal ban on noncitizen couldn’t be used to support Cox’s prosecution since the U.S. Constitution says that states generally determine voter eligibility.

The case focused on a 1996 federal law that generally prohibits from voting in federal elections, . Violating the law is punishable by up to a year in prison, a fine, or both.

In his ruling, Leibowitz cited Article I, Article II, and the 17th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, which he interpreted as reserving authority for the states to determine who is eligible to vote in federal elections.

“When you’re prosecuted based on a law that Congress did not have the authority to pass, the prosecution cannot stand,” Leibowitz wrote.

He said that Congress can regulate election procedures, but that authority does not generally extend to determining the electorate.

“To hold otherwise would allow Congress to establish and modify the parameters of its own special electorate, entirely divorced from what Florida or any other State may decide,” Leibowitz said. “That result is precisely what our federal constitutional republic does not allow.”

Leibowitz rejected prosecutors’ arguments that the federal law was valid because of congressional powers over immigration, foreign affairs, and election administration.

The ruling ended Cox’s federal prosecution for now, but left Florida’s citizenship requirement for voting intact and did not resolve her potential deportation by the federal government.

Department of Homeland Security General Counsel James Percival posted on X on Friday regarding the ruling, mocking politicians who have denied that noncitizens have voted in elections.

"A Biden appointed judge in Florida says that federal bans on noncitizen voting are unconstitutional. The thing that never happens is now 'constitutionally protected activity!'" Percival wrote.

The Florida ruling comes after the Supreme Court last week cleared the way for the Trump administration to use its revamped federal voter eligibility database to ensure that noncitizens do not vote in elections.

Hans von Spakovsky, Senior Legal Fellow at Advancing American Freedom, said in a statement on Friday regarding the ruling, "Judge David Leibowitz’s opinion that the federal law barring aliens from voting is unconstitutional is patently wrong. It is true that states have the constitutional authority to set the qualifications of citizens who are eligible as voters in federal elections. But he ignores the fact that in Article I, Section 8, Congress is given 100% authority over naturalization.

"In other words, Congress has plenary authority over the admittance of aliens and the standards under which they are allowed to be in the U.S. That gives the federal government the authority to ban aliens from voting or otherwise in any way participating in the democratic process," he continued, later adding, "This is an obviously wrong decision that will be squashed by the 11th Circuit Court of Appeals."

text:
Three families filed a nationwide class action lawsuit on September 28, 2026, in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. They are challenging an August executive order that would deny citizenship to certain children born in the United States.

Background

On June 30, 2026, the Supreme Court struck down President Trump’s January 2025 birthright citizenship order in Trump v. Barbara. The Court relied on United States v. Wong Kim Ark and reaffirmed that nearly everyone born here is a citizen, with only a few narrow exceptions.

On August 6, five weeks later, the President signed two new orders. These orders seek to include additional groups of children within the existing exceptions. Executive Order 14418 instructs agencies to deny citizenship recognition for a U.S.-born child when neither parent is a citizen and a parent:

Is classified as an “alien enemy.”

Works for a foreign government or an immunized international organization.

Paid to “purchase or access” citizenship, potentially including certain surrogacy arrangements.

Committed fraud to obtain citizenship.

Executive Order 14419, the second order, addresses birth tourism.

The Lawsuit

The plaintiffs are two couples working for international organizations on G-4 visas, and an Australian couple expecting a child via a U.S. surrogate. The ACLU and its partner organizations represent them. They say the President has no power to change the definition of citizenship. The complaint alleges violations of the Fourteenth Amendment and federal law, and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) failed to follow notice-and-comment rulemaking procedures.

Children affected could be denied passports and Social Security numbers, face removal or be at risk for statelessness, the complaint says. DHS defends the rule, noting that children of foreign government employees can register as permanent residents from birth.

What Families Should Know

The court has yet to rule on whether to block the order. Families should consult with legal counsel before applying for a child’s passport or Social Security number in the following situations:

Neither parent is a U.S. citizen, and a parent works for a foreign government or an international organization.

The family is planning a U.S. surrogacy.

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has launched a new tip line for citizens to report illegal immigrants with Commercial Driver’s Licenses (CDLs), citing a case in Massachusetts where a Haitian national living in Brockton allegedly hit and killed a Pennsylvania state trooper when his tractor trailer veered off a highway.

The tip line comes amid mounting concerns over illegal immigrants who may be substantially unqualified as CDL drivers, particularly when it comes to reading and understanding U.S. road signs that are written in English, and as serious accidents involving such drivers are seen across the country.

“Too many American lives have been lost or permanently changed because illegal aliens who have no business being on our roads have been granted CDLs. ICE and our federal partners, including the Department of Transportation, will be cracking down on CDL fraud so that not one more American life is lost to a reckless illegal alien behind the wheel of a semi-truck,” said Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin. “You can help save American lives and make our roads safer by dialing ICE’s new CDL fraud tipline today.”

ICE cited several high-profile cases involving accidents caused by illegal immigrant CDL drivers, including a Massachusetts case that resulted in the death of a Pennsylvania state trooper back in July, as its primary example.

The Herald had reported in July that Haitian national Michael Bon, 33, of Brockton, who had been in the country illegally since June 2025, allegedly hit and killed 44-year-old Pennsylvania State Trooper Michael Pahira when his tractor-trailer veered off I-81 in Schuylkill County and struck the trooper as he was conducting a routine commercial inspection on another tractor-trailer.

Bon faces involuntary manslaughter, homicide by vehicle, aggravated assault by vehicle, and reckless driving, among other charges.

The Commonwealth of Massachusetts issued Bon his CDL, with the U.S. Department of Transportation (USDOT) telling the Herald that state officials “fought every step of the way” against an emergency federal rule implemented in 2025 they say would have ultimately prevented Bon from renewing his CDL.

“In 2025, USDOT issued an emergency rule to strengthen federal oversight of how states issue non-domicile CDLs. But Massachusetts fought it every step of the way… and now is backing a lawsuit to block the final rule!” USDOT said in a post to its official X page in the days following the crash.

“This obstruction allowed Michael Bon to renew his commercial driver’s license DESPITE being in our nation illegally. USDOT and FMCSA are working EVERY DAY to change the policies to stop unqualified and unvetted foreign truck drivers from getting CDL’s,” it said.

The Trump administration, through the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA), implemented a new rule in September 2025 officially barring TPS holders, DACA recipients, asylum seekers, refugees, and other forms of noncitizens from obtaining, renewing or transferring a non-domiciled CDL.

The FMCSA, in a press release announcing the new rule, cited “widespread non-compliance” among state driver licensing agencies, including at the Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV), paired with an uptick in deadly crashes involving non-domiciled CDL holders.

In November 2025, Attorney General Campbell led 18 other attorneys general in Democratic-run states in supporting a lawsuit to end the new emergency rule, describing it as unlawful while adding it would “strip nearly all of the country’s 200,000 non-domiciled CLD holders of their licenses and their livelihoods.”

The RMV points the finger at the federal government, telling the Herald immediately following the crash that Bon was eligible for and received a non-domiciled CDL under federal standards at the time of his application in March 2025.

On July 2, 2024, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) admitted Bon into the United States at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport as a parolee. In October of that year, Bon filed an application for Temporary Protected Status (TPS) with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) under the Biden administration which ultimately was never granted. Last week, the Supreme Court ruled in favor of the federal government to end TPS for Haitian nationals.

In June of 2025. USCIS terminated Bon’s parole, issuing him a notice on June 13. But despite his parole being terminated, Bon refused to leave the country and remained in the United States illegally, settling in Brockton.

DHS has implemented other recent measures to combat illegal immigrant CDL drivers, including launching Joint Task Force Crossroads of America in August, described as an interagency effort to crack down on fraud in the trucking industry. In July, the department announced a new partnership to crack down on fraudulent and illegal practices in CDL schools across the country.

Citizens can report CDL fraud on the new tip line by dialing 866-347-2423.

text:
CHICAGO (WLS) -- Vehicle stops are one of the riskiest maneuvers for any law enforcement officer. But after men were killed by federal immigration agents in Texas, Maine and in the Chicago suburbs, the ABC7 I-Team has learned Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is changing its policy on who can stop vehicles.

According to sources familiar with the change who spoke with ABC News, ICE has announced a new vehicle stop policy that only those who have completed relevant training may participate in stops, and officers who initiate vehicle stops must have lights and sirens.

ABC7 Chicago is now streaming 24/7. Click here to watch

Nearly a year ago during the government's Midway Blitz in Chicago streets, many examples show that was not the standard used by agents.

It was Oct. 6, 2025, when harrowing video captured the moment federal immigration enforcers rammed into a vehicle driven by Chicagoan Marimar Martinez.

"Alright it's time to get aggressive," said Border Patrol Agent Charles Exum in recorded body-worn camera footage. "We're going to make contact."

Agent Exum opened fire, shooting Martinez five times in the Brighton Park neighborhood. Martinez survived but was arrested after DHS officials claimed she had boxed in the agents using her vehicle.

Video from the scene reviewed by the I-Team contradicts that claim and all charges against her were eventually dropped.

In another incident on Oct. 14, 2025, home surveillance cameras captured immigration agents in a high-speed pursuit through residential streets on Chicago's East Side. Forcing their target to crash after performing a PIT maneuver, a tactic law enforcement experts tell the I-Team could have endangered the public.

And in Franklin Park on Sept. 12, 2025, Silverio Villegas-Gonzalez was shot and killed by an ICE agent during an attempted vehicle stop.

These incidents and more across the country, including two recent fatal shootings in Texas and Maine, have led outside observers to question DHS policies surrounding vehicle stops and pursuits.

"We have seen a number of highly publicized instances captured on video where the tactics and techniques being used by these enforcement personnel conducting traffic stops really fall outside of accepted practice," said former Homeland Security official and ABC News contributor John Cohen.

Cohen told the I-Team this is a critical policy change.

"Any ICE personnel that is engaged in a traffic stop will be trained, will have properly equipped vehicle, will be wearing body worn camera the policy prohibits high speed pursuits, and it restricts the types of tactical stops that we've seen employed in the past," Cohen said.

The policy change will not only protect the public, but Cohen notes it will also keep DHS agents safe.

"If done improperly, it can result in the officer making the stop, the occupants of the vehicle, or a bystander being injured or killed," Cohen told the I-Team.

An ICE spokesperson claims the changes are "nothing new."

"Occasionally, ICE leadership issues guidance reminders to law enforcement officers," an ICE spokesperson said in an emailed statement. "This memo makes no changes to how ICE conducts vehicle stops. ALL officers have always received vehicle stop training."

"Vehicle stops and arrests of illegal aliens continue," the statement says.

ABC News contributed to this report.

title: María Elvira Salazar and her broken promise to half a million Cubans - EL PAÍS English
description:
María Elvira Salazar wore a dark blouse and a striking pearl necklace when she arrived at journalist Juan Manuel Cao’s studio in Miami.
“María Elvira is grasping at straws,” she shrugs.
A Trump ally is born After being defeated by Democratic Congresswoman Donna Shalala in 2018, Salazar decided to continue pursuing politics.
Her programs, such as María Elvira Confronta and María Elvira Live, turned her audience into her voters.
“María Elvira could have done more for them.”
text:
María Elvira Salazar wore a dark blouse and a striking pearl necklace when she arrived at journalist Juan Manuel Cao’s studio in Miami. She took a seat, tucked her hair behind her ears, made sure she had good lighting and found the best camera angle. She’s well trained in the ways of television.

“So, how’s the campaign going?” Cao asked her in Spanish. Salazar said everything was going well, but that she would get the real answer during the midterm elections, on November 3. Then, she addressed the camera directly and spoke to the residents of Florida’s 27th Congressional District: “And, if you want to vote for me, fantastic. I’d like you to vote for me so I can return [to Congress] and finish the job.”

Days earlier, Salazar had released a video, filmed in Washington, D.C., addressed to President Donald Trump, in which she warned him that his immigration policies had gone “too far.” She added that the same Hispanics who helped him win the White House in 2024 now felt “betrayed.”

May Díaz was at work when the congresswoman’s video appeared on her phone screen. “María Elvira is grasping at straws,” she shrugs. “She knows that the way she’s neglected her own community will stare her in the face come November.”

At one point, Díaz, 36, believed that, if there was a solution for people like her, it might come with Salazar’s help. “Not because I thought a single congresswoman could solve the I-220A situation with a stroke of the pen, but because she campaigned fueling that hope,” she clarifies. “She presented herself as our advocate: she spoke about legalization, solutions and dignity. But María Elvira has manipulated us all; she’s taken advantage of the uncertainty and fear that we live with.”

Five years ago, after participating in the largest anti-establishment protests in Cuba in July of 2021, Díaz left the island for the United States. She crossed the border and, when agents released her, they gave her a document that almost became a death sentence: an Order of Release on Recognizance, or an I-220A. This allowed her to enter the country, but not to become a permanent resident (as several generations of Cubans have done for decades).

In 2022, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) argued that the I-220A form doesn’t constitute a form of humanitarian parole. And, a year later, a federal court upheld that decision.

At the time, almost no Cuban really knew what it meant to have an I-220A. This category was established during the first Trump administration (2017-2021) and the document continued to be issued to thousands of people during the border crisis under Joe Biden’s presidency.

Whereas other groups of Cuban migrants had previously been dubbed Marielitos (referring to the exodus of 125,000 people from the port of Mariel in 1980) or “the rafters” (some 35,000 people who took to the sea in homemade rafts to cross the Florida Straits in the 1990s), the newest arrivals were called “the I-220As.” This group is part of the largest exodus since the Cuban Revolution of 1959. Nearly two million people have left Cuba over the past five years, fleeing the worst economic crisis of the Castro regime.

Neither lawyers nor immigration experts have an answer as to why some Cubans were granted this status and others were not (beyond pointing to the chaotic way in which the authorities were managing the border crossings). Congresswoman Salazar focused on these migrants and made them part of her rhetoric, in a state with more than 700,000 Cuban-American voters.

A Trump ally is born

After being defeated by Democratic Congresswoman Donna Shalala in 2018, Salazar decided to continue pursuing politics. And, during a rematch in 2020, she won the seat as the Republican candidate for Congress in Florida’s 27th District, promising to represent the diversity of a district that encompasses Latino neighborhoods like Little Havana, Pinecrest, and Kendall. “I have told my congressional leadership that it’s time for the Republican party to embrace the Hispanics back to the GOP. Some of the [immigration] enforcement that we have been creating in the last year (2020) is not the way,” she declared, when she won her primary.

Salazar was a fixture in Miami’s local media ecosystem for nearly three decades: a reporter for Channel 23 and Univision, a CNN correspondent, as well as an anchor for AméricaTeVé and MegaTV. She was a young, attractive face who made a name for herself on television with her coverage of the Salvadoran Civil War (1979-1992), her interview with Fidel Castro in New York City — which she described as the “most difficult” conversation she ever conducted — and her interview with Augusto Pinochet, which was the last one he ever gave.

Those who know her say that, if anything has defined Salazar, it’s her work ethic. Her programs, such as María Elvira Confronta and María Elvira Live, turned her audience into her voters. “Among my voters are many of the people I served during my 35 years as a member of the Spanish-language press,” she once said.

“She was a very well-known figure here. She had a very balanced image; she could reach a broad audience,” says journalist Roberto Céspedes, who worked with Salazar for several years as executive producer of some of her programs. It was Céspedes, the story goes, who once told her, “I think that, if you run for office, you’ll win.”

One day, he realized that the journalist was using her TV program to lay the groundwork for a career in politics. Up until then, according to several people close to her, she was quite moderate, liberal… and even traveled to Cuba.

“But I saw that she was starting to veer dramatically to the right, in favor of Trump. She secretly started running [for office], cultivating a conservative image,” Céspedes recounts. Trump, in turn, with a message on X (then Twitter), put his hand on her shoulder. “María is badly needed in Washington,” he said. “Maria has my Complete & Total Endorsement!”

The daughter of Cuban immigrants, Salazar was born in Miami and grew up in Puerto Rico, speaking English with a strong accent. In recent years, she has spoken about the “evils” of socialism and has fervently criticized the Democratic Party’s policies. She has promised to fight to lower taxes and solve the housing crisis, while consolidating her position within the Cuban-American lobby in Washington.

“At the same time — being aware of the remarkable diversity of the electorate in the 27th District, which includes significant communities of Central and South American immigrants — she’s tried to position herself as an advocate for other Latin American groups, especially Venezuelans. This combination of loyalty to the Cuban exile community and attention to new waves of migration has decisively shaped her political profile in South Florida,” says Jorge Duany, former director of the Institute of Cuban Studies and professor emeritus at Florida International University.

On several occasions, Salazar has publicly pledged to help the nearly 500,000 Cuban migrants who have been issued Form I-220A. In fact, she heavily criticized the Biden administration over this issue.

“We’re talking about half a million people who have families who are voters,” Céspedes points out.

Salazar’s supporters agree that, throughout this time, among the three Cuban-American Republican members of Congress from Florida — along with Mario Díaz-Balart and Carlos A. Giménez — she’s been the most supportive of migrants. Her detractors, however, maintain that her support for those issued Form I-220A was more of a campaign against Biden, rather than a campaign in favor of the thousands of people left in legal limbo.

Earlier this year, Salazar sent letters to Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, explaining that it’s currently impossible for this group of migrants to benefit from the 1966 Cuban Adjustment Act, which allows Cubans to become American residents and pursue citizenship.

Salazar has said that this “trash paper” — referring to Form I-220A — was given to Cubans by Biden; she called it “an empty promise” and asserted that Trump was “cleaning up Biden’s political mess.” She even said that she discussed the issue with former DHS secretary Kristi Noem, urging her to consider the I-220A document as proof of legal entry for Cubans.

Over her past six years in Washington, the congresswoman has asked Cubans who hold this document to trust her: “What I can say is that there’s hope.” And, last year, she again raised expectations with the new Trump administration: “We have four years to prove that Republicans can help [those who have been issued] Form I-220A.”

However, as time has passed, Cubans holding I-220As have begun to doubt the congresswoman’s claims. EL PAÍS contacted Salazar’s office about this, but her team responded that she was “not available at this time” for an interview.

“A political game”

“What María Elvira and the other congresspeople have done is nothing more than a political game to benefit themselves,” says José Gutiérrez, a 43-year-old Cuban who has been living in the United States since 2022. He holds an I-220A.

Gutiérrez, an Uber driver, has had to change his routine. He doesn’t dare go out in the mornings; he’s afraid of being the next Cuban to be apprehended by immigration agents in Florida, the state with the most arrests in 2025.

“I’m suffering from panic attacks and anxiety. I’m taking medication and seeing a psychiatrist,” he sighs. “I haven’t seen any pressure being put on politicians in Congress or on the president to find a real solution… not only for the I-220As, but for all the Cubans who are currently in legal limbo,” Gutiérrez laments.

However, Congresswoman Salazar asserts that, if anyone is doing anything for these migrants, it’s her.

During her recent appearance on journalist Juan Manuel Cao’s program, she recounted that, during a 10-minute phone call with Trump, she told him that she wasn’t attacking him with her recent statements. Rather, she was offering him advice. “It’s up to you,” Salazar claims that she told him. “I’ve done my part to explain what’s happening.”

Salazar’s words sparked a backlash that united various sectors of the MAGA community, some Washington politicians, the DHS (which affirmed that it will continue enforcing the law “whether Congresswoman Salazar likes it or not”)... and even migrants who feel like they’ve been political pawns in her campaign. This is especially true for those holding I-220As: they know that much time has passed without any change in their circumstances.

“I support Republican values. I’m a Christian, I’m a conservative… but seeing María Elvira Salazar express herself this way — when she’s practically lost the Hispanic vote, due to how she’s neglected them in recent years — raises a lot of red flags for me,” says 32-year-old Manuel Alberto Guerra, a doctor who arrived in the U.S. from Cuba back in 2022. While he was able to get his medical degree validated in Florida, the fact that he holds an I-220A has limited his job opportunities and his chances of earning better wages.

The polls being conducted ahead of the November midterm elections show Salazar in a tie with her Democratic opponent. And Esteban Rodríguez — a Cuban political activist who suffered repression on the island — has no doubt that the congresswoman is talking about people like him “because she needs the votes of the Cubans in her district.” Holding an I-220A, he remains in an irregular situation in Miami.

“But she had plenty of time to do a little more for the I-220As,” Rodríguez points out. “This is a maneuver; I don’t think she intends to help the I-220As or resolve the immigration status of all of us who are stuck in limbo.”

“She’s no friend of immigrants”

Activist Thomas Kennedy hasn’t forgotten the day that Salazar visited the notorious South Florida Detention Facility (nicknamed “Alligator Alcatraz”) last year, back when he was part of a campaign to close it.

“She inspected the site… and when she left, she defended it, saying it met the highest federal standards,” he recalls. “She’s not a trustworthy person,” he asserts. “She’s no friend of immigrants.”

Olga Soto’s partner — who suffers from diabetes — was imprisoned at the Krome Detention Center in Miami-Dade Country. She remembers the countless emails that she sent to Salazar’s office seeking help. They never responded. “The lawyers said the only reason I could call my congresswoman was because his life was in danger,” she says. “She never even spoke to me.”

Some criticize Salazar, along with the two other Cuban-American congresspeople, for voting in favor of a $70 billion funding package for the DHS, effectively approving increased funding for Trump’s immigration enforcement.

The bill introduced by Salazar back in 2023 — the “Dignity for Immigrants while Guarding our Nation to Ignite and Deliver the American Dream Act,” or the DIGNIDAD Act — has also been poorly received. In addition to a proposal to secure the U.S.-Mexico border, it includes provisions allowing undocumented immigrants who arrived in the country in the last five years to obtain temporary legal status to work (provided that they pay the government $7,000 in “restitution”). However, this law wouldn’t grant them the possibility of obtaining either U.S. permanent residency or citizenship.

“There’s no path [offered by the bill] that truly leads to a dignified life,” says May Díaz. “What’s being offered is a conditional, expensive [immigration] status, [with people being] subjected to surveillance, without any guarantees of a permanent future [in the U.S]. It turns people into captive labor.”

But what most upsets some lawyers and analysts in South Florida is that, according to them, GOP Representatives Salazar, Diaz-Balart, and Giménez had ample opportunity to legalize immigrants who were issued Form I-220A… and they failed to do so.

Last year, when the House voted on Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which would define the administration’s budget, the three of them had the ability to exercise power with their votes. The legislation ultimately only passed by one vote (215-214).

“In the vote on the annual U.S. budget in the House of Representatives, those three votes together could have been [leveraged] to make a change regarding immigrants holding I-220A forms… but it didn’t happen,” Florida immigration lawyer Willy Allen laments. “María Elvira could have done more for them.”
