title: Renee Good's family sues Trump administration over fatal ICE shooting - Al Jazeera
description:
The family of Renee Good, one of two US citizens fatally shot by federal immigration agents in the state of Minnesota, has sued the government over her killing during a sweeping immigrant deportation blitz in January.
The lawsuits are the first major civil actions taken against the Trump administration over its unprecedented deportation crackdowns in Minneapolis last winter, dubbed Operation Metro Surge.
Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defence and that Good had engaged in “an act of domestic terrorism”.
Minnesota sued the Trump administration in March to gain access to the evidence it gathered at the shooting scenes, but investigations stalled after the Justice Department halted its routine cooperation and evidence-sharing with the Minneapolis Police Department.
None of the agents involved in Good’s killing has faced any charges.
text:
The family of Renee Good, one of two US citizens fatally shot by federal immigration agents in the state of Minnesota, has sued the government over her killing during a sweeping immigrant deportation blitz in January.

The two lawsuits – filed on Thursday by Good’s partner, Becca Good, and Renee’s brother, Brent Ganger – say officials from US President Donald Trump’s administration were reckless and violated the civil rights of Good and others in Minneapolis. The lawsuits are demanding a jury trial and financial damages.

The lawsuits are the first major civil actions taken against the Trump administration over its unprecedented deportation crackdowns in Minneapolis last winter, dubbed Operation Metro Surge.

The first lawsuit seeks damages for Good’s wrongful death under Minnesota law, citing claims of assault, battery, false imprisonment, negligence and intentional infliction of emotional distress.

The second lawsuit alleges a civil rights conspiracy among numerous defendants including the immigration officer and shooter Jonathon Ross, who was named alongside high-ranking Trump administration officials, including White House Deputy Policy Chief Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, former Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino and Trump’s longtime campaign adviser, Corey Lewandowski.

Good, a mother of three, was shot and killed in her car by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent in south Minneapolis when she and her wife joined one of the city’s daily demonstrations against masked and armed federal agents deployed to the city to arrest migrants for deportation.

Widespread cellphone footage taken by eyewitnesses captured the moment in which Good was killed, after agent Ross fired into the windshield, shooting her in the head, arm and torso.

Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defence and that Good had engaged in “an act of domestic terrorism”.

In a statement posted on Truth Social at the time, Trump defended the deadly ICE shooting, saying that the reason those “incidents” were happening was that “the Radical Left is threatening, assaulting, and targeting our Law Enforcement Officers and ICE Agents on a daily basis”.

Days after the shooting, officials from the US Department of Justice, including then-Deputy Attorney Todd Blanche, blocked federal prosecutors from pursuing a criminal civil rights case against the agents involved in her killing, which prompted at least half a dozen of those prosecutors to resign in protest.

Minnesota sued the Trump administration in March to gain access to the evidence it gathered at the shooting scenes, but investigations stalled after the Justice Department halted its routine cooperation and evidence-sharing with the Minneapolis Police Department.

None of the agents involved in Good’s killing has faced any charges.

text:
WASHTENAW COUNTY, Mich. — A Trinity Health Ann Arbor nurse is facing a federal criminal charge after prosecutors say she helped an immigration detainee escape from the hospital while he was in U.S. Border Patrol custody.

Chloe Renae Freeman has been charged with one count of instigating or assisting escape, a misdemeanor that carries up to one year in prison. She has pleaded not guilty. Her next court date is Oct. 20.

Freeman made her initial court appearance in Detroit on Tuesday and was released on a $10,000 unsecured bond.

You can watch Ruta Ulcinaite's full report below:

Ann Arbor nurse charged with helping ICE detainee escape from Trinity Health hospital

According to a federal criminal complaint filed Aug. 28 in the Eastern District of Michigan, U.S. Border Patrol agents conducted a targeted immigration enforcement operation on May 28 in Ann Arbor. Agents approached the man, identified in court documents only by the initials OBP, near the intersection of Washtenaw Avenue and Pittsfield Boulevard. OBP is described as a native and citizen of Mexico who had previously been removed from the United States on or about Dec. 12, 2022, from Arizona.

When agents approached OBP, they claim he fled, tripped over a curb and hit his face on the pavement. After agents took him into custody, they observed bleeding from his head and contacted Emergency Medical Services. EMS transported OBP to Trinity Health Ann Arbor Hospital for further evaluation.

The complaint states that after OBP completed a CT scan, Freeman came to the CT scan room and told the operator to hold OBP and not return him to his room. Badge swipe data from the hospital showed Freeman accessed the second-floor CT Room on May 28. Security video footage then showed OBP exiting the hospital through the ambulance bay door.

The complaint states that during a hospital interview on June 18, Freeman admitted to letting OBP leave. She said she knew he was an ICE custody patient but claimed she did not believe he was in custody at the time because ICE agents were not physically with him in the CT room. The complaint states Freeman removed OBP's IV and escorted him out through the ambulance bay doors before he was properly discharged and before his hospital care was complete.

The complaint states Freeman told investigators she did not agree with ICE separating people from their families and that she "knew she was going to set him free." Law enforcement has been unable to locate OBP since his escape from the hospital.

Immigration attorney at Atiya Law, Shahad Atiya, who is also a professor at UM Dearborn, said the charge against Freeman is unusual.

"It's alleging a violation of federal law, a misdemeanor violation that could carry up to one year in prison," Atiya said. "We haven't seen it yet in the space where we deal with immigration offenses. I think this is going to be probably a new set of charges that are targeting people who are looking to assist immigrants in one way or another," Atiya said.

Diego Bonesatti, legal services program manager with Michigan United, said his organization has been tracking ICE arrests across Michigan and that the incident in Washtenaw County does not surprise him.

"Given the lack of training of new ICE recruits and the massive amount of spending and hiring, it does not surprise me that people are getting hurt," Bonesatti said.

Laura Sanders, co-founder of the Movement for Immigrant Rights Action or MIRA, says the defendant has her organization, and others, in her corner.

"We as advocates and activists in this area have respect for her attempt to protect this immigrant man," Sanders said.

Trinity Health Ann Arbor released a statement regarding the incident:

"The individual referenced is no longer employed by Trinity Health Ann Arbor. Because this is an active legal matter, we are unable to comment on the specific allegations or ongoing court proceedings."

The criminal complaint was filed by FBI Special Agent Michael Wagner and signed by U.S. Magistrate Judge Kimberly Altman. The case was initially sealed before being unsealed ahead of Freeman's court appearance.

text:
MINNEAPOLIS -- Renee Good's family sued the U.S. government and several immigration officials Thursday, alleging wrongful death, conspiracy and other violations in the 37-year-old woman's killing by an immigration officer during a federal crackdown in Minneapolis.

The two lawsuits were filed by Good's partner, Becca Good, and Renee's brother Brent Ganger.

"She was pure love. She was funny. She was smart," Becca Good said during a news conference to announce the lawsuits. "She was the center of my universe."

The Justice Department didn't immediately respond to an email seeking comment.

Officer shot Good as she turned her car away from him

Renee Good was fatally shot Jan. 7 as protests against immigration raids flared across the city. According to Becca Good, her partner stopped their car in a street to support neighbors during an immigration operation.

Bystander video shows Renee Good in the driver's seat of a red SUV blocking part of the road and repeatedly honking her horn.

Two immigration officers get out of a truck, their faces covered, and one orders Good to get out of the car. She reverses briefly, then turns the steering wheel as the officer says again, "get out of the car."

Almost simultaneously, Becca Good, standing in the street, shouts: "Drive, baby, drive!"

One officer standing in front of the vehicle pulls his weapon and fires into the windshield. He lurches back as the car turns away from him. The officer, who is now very close to the open window on the driver's side, fires two more times, fatally shooting Renee Good, according to an analysis of the videos by The Associated Press and others.

Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defense and that Good had engaged in "an act of domestic terrorism."

One lawsuit alleges wrongful death

The lawsuit against the United States of America seeks damages for Good's wrongful death and "the immense suffering Renee endured in the final moments of her life and for the profound and permanent losses that her death has inflicted upon her family," according to a news release by lawyers for Ganger and Good.

The lawsuit, which seeks a bench trial, also alleges "intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligent infliction of emotional distress" on Becca Good.

Becca and Renee Good, the mother of three children, were not legally married, according to a family lawyer, but referred to one another as wives. They had only recently relocated to Minneapolis from Kansas City, Missouri.

Another lawsuit alleges conspiracy to conceal evidence

The other lawsuit alleges a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights and seeks a jury trial. It says the federal government moved to hide the evidence of what actually happened on Jan. 7.

The lawsuit says the shots fired by Jonathan Ross, the immigration officer who killed Good, "were the predictable and intended product of the operation."

It describes a "carefully planned, coordinated effort between senior federal officials and private actors to make two ethnic communities — Minnesotans of Somali and Hispanic descent and origin — the object of aggression and abduction, and to silence by intimidation, arrest and violence the neighbors and allies of those targeted communities who observed, documented and warned of that campaign."

The lawsuit names Ross as a defendant, as well as: White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller; former Homeland Security head Kristi Noem; Corey Lewandowski, a campaign manager for President Donald Trump who also served as one of Noem's advisers; White House border czar Tom Homan; former acting director of U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement Todd Lyons; former U.S. Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino; and 10 unnamed federal agents.

Good's partner acknowledges other lives lost in immigration crackdown

The killing of Good and another U.S. citizen, Alex Pretti, in Minneapolis just weeks later sparked outrage across the country and calls to rein in immigration enforcement. At least 10 people have died in encounters with immigration officers during President Donald Trump's second term.

In social media accounts, Renee Good described herself as a "poet and writer and wife and mom." On Pinterest, a profile picture shows her smiling and holding a young child, alongside posts about tattoos, hairstyles and home decorating.

In an interview shortly after her death, Renee Good's mother, Donna Ganger, told The Associated Press: "She had this way of making you feel special and loved that I didn't even understand that until we lost her."

Good's partner noted the broader loss to communities nationwide.

"As we have tried to navigate our own massive loss, I am also devastated by how many other lives have been destroyed in this darkest of times," Becca Good said in the news release Thursday. "So many other families are dealing with the loss of their loved ones; to everyone who has had to witness it — the pain of this moment extends far beyond our family. What happened to us should never happen to any family."

McCormack reported from Concord, New Hampshire.

text:
A preliminary injunction is a temporary court order issued before a case is finally decided that requires a party to take or stop an action while the litigation continues. Federal courts generally consider likelihood of success, irreparable harm, the balance of equities, and the public interest before granting one.

A preliminary injunction is a form of temporary judicial relief designed to protect the parties or preserve meaningful relief while a lawsuit is pending.

Unlike a final judgment, a preliminary injunction is issued before the court has fully resolved the merits of the case.

In federal civil litigation, preliminary injunctions are governed by Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 65. State courts have their own procedural rules and standards.

What Must Someone Show to Obtain a Preliminary Injunction?

The Supreme Court set out the modern federal framework in Winter v. Natural Resources Defense Council.

A party seeking a preliminary injunction generally must establish a likelihood of success on the merits, a likelihood of irreparable harm without preliminary relief, that the balance of equities favors the requested order, and that an injunction is in the public interest.

The Supreme Court has emphasized that a preliminary injunction is an extraordinary remedy, not something a party receives automatically just because a lawsuit has been filed.

What Is Irreparable Harm?

Irreparable harm generally means an injury that cannot be adequately corrected through ordinary legal relief after the case is finished.

In Winter, the Supreme Court rejected a standard based merely on the possibility of irreparable injury. The party seeking relief ordinarily must establish that the injury is likely in the absence of an injunction.

Preliminary Injunctions and Death Penalty Litigation

Preliminary injunctions sometimes play a central role in method-of-execution litigation.

A prisoner facing an execution date can seek an injunction preventing officials from using a disputed procedure while the constitutional challenge is litigated. Because the execution would make later judicial relief impossible, questions of irreparable harm are particularly significant.

The prisoner must still satisfy the standards governing extraordinary equitable relief, including a sufficient showing on the underlying constitutional claim.

Preliminary Injunction Versus Final Injunction

A preliminary injunction operates while litigation remains pending.

A permanent injunction is entered after the court resolves the legal dispute and determines that permanent equitable relief is appropriate.

Granting preliminary relief does not mean the party seeking the injunction will ultimately win the case.

irreparable harm

text:
For 25-year-old Catherine Rax, another day inside a cell at the Flagler County Jail is another day spent wondering what comes next.

“It’s not living — it’s surviving,” she told the Tallahassee Democrat.

You may not recognize her name. You may not even remember her face at the local eatery. But you have seen her before — in headlines, across social media, in that traumatic moment captured on surveillance video. A moment that would change her life and the lives of those around her forever.

On Friday, Sept. 25, a traffic stop that escalated into an immigration-enforcement operation at beloved local food establishment Chile & Chili's Taqueria became the center of a broader conversation about immigration enforcement in Tallahassee.

Days later, nearly 100 local community members rallied around the Mexican eatery at its now permanently closed West Tennessee Street location with the help of the Tallahassee Community Area Response Equipo (TCARE), which is the Leon County hub for the Florida Immigrant Coalition as well as the Tallahassee Immigrant Rights Alliance.

Wednesday night made it evident that the space that once served as a designated hangout spot to indulge in a taste of Oaxaca and catch up with friends has been stained with the events of that day.

"The people united... will never be defeated," the crowd chanted as they held signs and waved their flags. Children and elders, students and young professionals of every background gathered in front of the trucks that Wednesday night.

Among them were Rax’s friends, who held up a tablet so she could see the crowd gathered in her honor. From inside the jail, she watched the community rally around her, an attempt to lift her spirits and remind her that people cared.

While that 20-second surveillance video may make the impact feel distant, the Tallahassee Democrat came face-to-face with Rax through a tablet inside the county jail. For 10 emotional minutes, she shared her story before the call timed out.

"Honestly, I’m very sad… they’re not just my coworkers; they’re my family," Rax said, clinging to the phone for strength as she held back tears. Rax has no immediate family with her in Tallahassee.

Rax worked the stand, where coworkers had become some of the people she leaned on most.

Every dollar she earned carried more weight as her mother battles cancer, she'd often send the money she made back home to help with the family and medical expenses. Before her detention, survival meant showing up to work, helping her family and making it through another day. From inside the walls of the county jail, survival looks a lot different.

Now, Rax is separated from her family and loved ones, waiting inside the county jail, and she has no idea what awaits.

"What questions do I have? I have so many. When am I going to get out of here? How long am I going to last here? How long will I be here? When will I be able to see my family?… I didn't ask to be illegal," Rax said.

Along with Rax, two men were detained, including her partner.

One of them is now in the state-run immigration detention facility nicknamed "Deportation Depot" in Baker County. All three were originally from Guatemala.

"We were a family … always cheerful, always dancing, there was always music, working, and cooking … wholesome, good-hearted people. Remembering the innocence of such good people, what is happening hurts deep in the soul," Chile & Chili's owner Marco Tenorio said.

Hours after the rally, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) sent a statement to the Tallahassee Democrat confirming the operation, stating that they did not "target the taqueria" and the three detained at the taco stand "attempted to flee" and "entered the United States illegally."

"They don't realize the mental harm they are causing, and that all of this will have consequences … But on the other hand, I feel very good about how the people are supporting us. The outpouring of support has been incredible … it gives you that feeling where you say to yourself, 'I did something right,' " Tenorio said.

Zolia Virgen Verduzco, by way of Quincy, made her way through the crowds, thanking individuals for showing their support.

For Verduzco, the rally hit close to home; just recently, her brother, who lived in the country for 45 years, was detained and deported to Mexico, she says, despite having legal counsel and documentation processes underway, and thousands she's paid in legal fees.

"It means a lot to us because sometimes it feels good to know that someone cares," she said. "I really feel, honestly, that it's time for all of us to get together, to be united."

text:
North Carolina’s first immigration detention center is set to open in the state’s northeastern corner before year’s end. Though activists have protested against the center, some residents say they don’t sense that opposition in their communities and look forward to the facility’s projected economic gains.

The GEO Group, one of the world’s largest federal prison contractors and owner of Rivers Correctional Institution in Winton, said in July that it signed a five-year contract with Immigration and Customs Enforcement to reopen the 1,320-bed facility this year as Winton ICE Processing Center.

The facility lies on the edge of Hertford County, about 20 miles south of the Virginia state line; it’s surrounded by trees and rural farmland. The facility closed in 2021 after President Joe Biden issued an executive order to terminate all federal contracts with private prisons.

Before it closed, Rivers had high rates of inmate grievances, positive drug tests and inmate-on-inmate sexual assault according to a 2016 federal report. However, it employed hundreds of people, and some locals The News & Observer interviewed said the pay was enough to support middle-class lifestyles.

In July, an unnamed state official told The New York Times, which first reported the center’s opening, that it could open as early as late September. But the center had yet to open as October arrived. Construction continued near the front gate and 47 job postings were on The GEO Group’s careers page.

Rainier Bradshaw, 15, who lives in Winton and Murfreesboro — Hertford County towns with a combined population of less than 4,000 — started protesting the center earlier this year, speaking at a county commissioners meeting. She was scared to express herself so publicly, she said, but seeing others coming together to oppose the center gave her hope that they could stop the soon-to-be-detention center’s progress.

At a local protest Saturday, Bradshaw said it might now be “a little too late to hope that it’s not going to open at all.”

She added, “I hope that maybe something can be done quickly after it opens to close it again, or that it won’t just be another place of pain and suffering.”

ICE facility isn’t ‘on the radar’ for many locals

On Saturday, workers at the facility stood behind the entrance gate and watched as 50 protesters marched up and down the country road leading to the Winton facility.

But many of the protesters weren’t locals. During the march, they shouted out the places from which they’d come — Wilmington; the Outer Banks; Chapel Hill; Durham; Jones County; Virginia.

Ray Bradshaw, 55, Rainier’s father, said he wouldn’t be surprised if most locals didn’t know that the center was reopening as an ICE facility. When he speaks to people in town, it never comes up in conversation, he said.

Alison Brown, 58, who lives in Winton and Richmond, said Monday that neither she nor her husband, Mark Brown, had heard about Saturday’s protest before it happened.

“For it to be 50 people … that tells me that it wasn’t on the radar for the citizens around here,” she said.

Mark Brown said: “If (protesters from out of town) don’t live in this area … a lot of them are probably not impacted.”

Organizations beyond Hertford County have propelled the movement opposing the prison’s conversion detention center. Stop Detention Centers NC, a statewide grassroots organization, collected donations to pay for a $1,100 billboard in Ahoskie condemning the center earlier this year. They have also sent postcards to residents with a message echoing the billboard.

Jessica Burroughs, an organizer at The Workers Circle, a national nonprofit promoting social justice, said that her group’s advocacy is “just getting started” and that by continuing to protest, activists will draw locals’ eyes.

“Our criticism for the facility is not criticism of the people who are taking these jobs because they need the income. They are not the enemy here,” Burroughs said. “Our focus is on these private facilities and how much money is being given to those folks at the top running these institutions.”

Caroline Stephenson, a Hertford County resident and the protest’s primary organizer, said that as the center’s opening nears, protesters will keep marching, at least once a month.

The GEO Group did not respond to repeated requests for comment by The News & Observer.

Some locals see center’s economic opportunities

Mark Brown, 65, said he remembers getting paid to pick tobacco as a teenager.

“My whole family worked in the field,” Brown said. “Everyone got the experience of hard work.”

But as technology and farming equipment advanced, “it cut generations of people with jobs off,” he said. That makes bringing jobs like the ones at Winton ICE Processing Center all the more important, he said.

When Rivers was open, he said, people who worked there could make enough money to buy homes and have a good quality of life, Brown said. The closure cost 350 workers their jobs.

The facility had a job fair in August. Some former workers at Rivers have received communication from The GEO Group inviting them to return.

However, 10 of the 43 jobs Winston-based jobs listed on The GEO Group’s website that are based in Winton pay less than $42,000 a year, $3,000 shy of Hertford County’s median income, although salaries for detention center-related medical jobs, such as dentists, physicians and nurses, reach six figures.

Donnie Taylor, 75, a retired lawyer who lives in Bertie County, just 2 miles from the Hertford County border, said he doesn’t hear any complaints about the center, calling them “rumors.” With limited job opportunities in the area, he believes that the jobs it will bring should overshadow concerns.

“Anything coming to the area is good,” he said. “The people in the community where I live … my contacts and what I deal with … there isn’t just outrage for ICE.”

Taylor said he believes that “there’s more to worry about down here” than the detention center. He said more focus should be committed to addressing violent crime, gangs and drugs and that he wouldn’t mind having more law enforcement present in the area, even if it’s immigration authorities.

Numbers show crime rising in Hertford County. In 2023, the latest year with available data, the county, population 19,000, had 60 incidents of violent crime, a 30% increase from a year earlier, a 2025 report by the state’s Department of Public Safety shows. During the same period, Bertie County had 57 violent crimes, up 16% from a year earlier. The department broadly defines violent crimes as homicide, aggravated assault and rape.

Crime statistics notwithstanding, Ahoskie native Bobby Ray Riddick was warier of the detention center than Taylor. He said he’d cut ties with anyone who chooses to work there.

“What if it was your child that was being locked up?” said Riddick, who has protested against the center. “So you feel that the money, it outweighs someone that’s being incarcerated (wrongfully)?”

‘Most important contributor’ to the NC anti-detention center movement

Riddick, 62, started frequently driving by the center, livestreaming to his 10,000 followers on Facebook earlier this year. He said he’s not afraid of any local blowback.

“When you start talking about what’s going on in a community and people are scared to speak out because it’s being run by people who are from here that’s holding positions and they use their authority to intimidate people,” Riddick said. “I’m retired. I don’t have anything to lose. … So, I can freely speak up to how I feel without threat.”

Liz Dreesen, an organizer with Stop Detention Centers NC, said Riddick has boosted her group’s advocacy.

“Everybody tunes in to Bobby Ray because Bobby Ray does a lot of talking about what’s going on in the … Hertford County world,” Dreesen said. “Having Bobby Ray talk us up is probably the most important contributor to people knowing about what we’re doing.”

There’s more to the region than an ICE center, locals say

Booker Daniel, 67, who opposes the ICE facility, grew up near Stephenson, one of the movement’s primary organizers. Their homes in Murfreesboro were near a deep gully filled with sprawling trees and kudzu. They called themselves “gully girls.”

Daniel, a retired social worker, said she promised herself years ago to not work at Rivers.

“I’m glad I made that choice,” she said. “Not all money is good money.”

Daniel supports Stephenson in her movement against the detention center, though she understands why people want jobs there.

“Everything is so expensive right now,” she said.

Although the town is making headlines for the detention center, Daniel said that she wants “people to know that there’s more out here than the ICE facility.”

Once a month, she leads “Storytelling for Grown Folk,” a session at which she teaches about the town’s history to adults at the library.

Daniel said she enjoys talking about historic Murfreesboro, especially Murfrees Landing, a now defunct port and mill site that was once Murfreesboro’s claim to fame. She loves telling the story of Hannah Crafts, an enslaved woman famous for writing a novel during her enslavement, whose historic home is just a few minutes’ drive from where the Daniels’ family home had been.

That history is what she wants the region to be known for.

text:
“When UN Member States unanimously adopted the two great human rights Covenants 60 years ago, they brought the force of law to the principles set out in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR),” said UN Human Rights Chief Volker Türk.

On 17 September 2026, during its 63rd session, the Human Rights Council held a high-level panel in the Palais des Nations to mark 60 years of the International Covenants on Civil and Political Rights and on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICCPR and ICESCR). The Covenants were adopted on 16 December 1966. UN Human Rights’ campaign, “The Covenants at 60: A Commitment to Human Dignity,” extends through and beyond that date this year.

“After the 20th century’s paroxysms of war and genocide, States knew they must devise a system strong enough to uphold human rights across regions and generations,” Türk said.

It took almost 20 years to turn the UDHR into binding law. Cold War divisions split the single draft into two treaties in 1951, but both were adopted under one resolution.

“Above all, these rights are a safeguard against the abuse of power. The Covenant sets limits on what States may and may not do, regardless of political circumstances or expediency,” said Changrok Soh, panellist at the event and Chair of the Human Rights Committee.

Sixty years of impact

“[The] set of norms which were quite open ended and sometimes not especially clear and set of implementation arrangements which were really rudimentary have come to fruition in the form of a very solid normative consensus that underpins the human rights system and a very solid and effective Treaty Body system. It’s a huge achievement,” said Philip Alston, a panellist at the event, a New York University law professor and former Chair of the Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (CESCR).

A whole architecture grew from the Covenants: seven further core treaties, the Treaty Bodies, UN Human Rights, and the Council itself.

“The Covenants have notably inspired the Inter-American, African and the European human rights systems, as well as the ASEAN and Arab human rights Charters. Numerous domestic laws have drawn on the language of the treaties, from Colombia to the Philippines, Romania, South Africa, and many more,” Türk added.

Each Covenant has its own watchdog: the Human Rights Committee for the ICCPR and the Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights for the ICESCR, each made up of 18 independent experts. States parties report to them regularly and are reviewed in public dialogues that end in recommendations; the Committees also interpret the treaties through General Comments and, for states that have accepted the Optional Protocols, hear complaints from individuals who say their rights have been violated.

Türk explained how the two Committees ensure the continued relevance of the Covenants by applying them in regard to new developments and emerging issues. He said that for example in 2020, the Human Rights Committee made clear that the right of peaceful assembly applies to online gatherings, and in 2019, that same Committee found that States may not deport people to their countries of origin if they would face life-threatening impacts of climate change.

“In 2017, the Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights said States must adopt measures to prevent businesses from abusing peoples’ rights — and if people do suffer corporate abuses, States are responsible for providing them with effective remedy,” Türk added.

Preeti Saran, a panellist at the event and Chair of CESCR said that the ICESCR has inspired national courts and constitutions worldwide to treat socio-economic guarantees as enforceable rights, linked to the right to life.

For Soh, the two Covenants have transformed the international human rights landscape and converted rights from charity to legal entitlement; from beneficiaries to rights-holders; from a hierarchy of rights to indivisibility and interdependence; from abstract principles to concrete remedies; and from domestic issues to legitimate international concerns.

Indivisibility: the unfinished promise

Türk said that economic, social and cultural rights are as vital as civil and political rights, and that all these rights depend on each other, contributing to a virtuous circle of greater social cohesion, more trust in institutions, and more stability.

However, Alston said that in practice there is not an equal relationship between the two sets of rights and that the system remains absolutely dominated by attention given to civil and political rights.

According to Alston, only about 20 per cent of the Universal Periodic Review recommendations concern economic, social and cultural rights, and most of those are generic. These rights barely register at the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.

“As we struggle with the resurgence of populism in a great many countries, as we struggle to respond with the lowering standard of living of workers around the world, […] human rights have a very weak response because economic and social rights have not been given the status or the importance that they deserve,” Alston said.

Today’s threats

“Artificial intelligence, mass surveillance, biometric technologies pose new challenges to privacy, while disinformation spreads at a scale we have never seen. These developments raise questions of power and accountability,” Soh said.

He added that technological power has become dangerously concentrated in the hands of a few States, individuals and companies.

“Artificial intelligence and digital platforms are reshaping work, social protection, and access to services,” Saran said. “The same technologies are driving an unprecedented concentration of economic and political power. These developments demonstrate the need to rethink current economic models.”

Saran added that global oligopolies increasingly control goods and services, essential in the realization of covenant rights, including medicines, food supply, and digital infrastructure. The COVID pandemic revealed open discrimination in access to vaccines and to travel.

“Concentration of wealth and market power is not merely an economic fact, but a human rights challenge,” Saran said.

Alston warned that the single most important new actor in the entire human rights field, the private sector, can basically ignore human rights considerations.

A system at risk

“Today, I am extremely concerned that the entire human rights Treaty Body system is at risk of crumbling,” Türk said. “Cuts in funds have forced a sharp reduction in staff, cancellation of Committee country visits and sessions, and increasing delays in the consideration of States’ reports and people’s individual petitions for help.”

Saran said that 40 per cent budget cut, along with a drastic reduction in their meeting time and cancellation of the Committee’s pre-sessional working group, had made it harder to fulfil their mandate.

Soh emphasized that no reform is possible without resources.

“We urgently need to fulfil the commitment that States made in the Pact for the Future, to ensure adequate and sustained resources for all mandated work of the Treaty Body system,” Türk said.

“We also need reforms. The Treaty Bodies can become more accessible, efficient and impactful — if the resources are there,” Türk added.

Saran stressed that the only way to strengthen the system is to fund it adequately from the UN regular budget, so it can work without compromising its integrity and independence.

Soh said that Chairpersons are not against any change, not against reform, but reform needs to be done in a way that strengthens the Treaty Bodies.

text:
Key events

White House blocks CNN from press pool again, despite judge’s block on ban

The White House has, again, blocked CNN from covering Donald Trump as part of the rotating press pool.

The outlet was scheduled to be a part of the group of media traveling to Texas and Oklahoma with the president today, but was removed from list of newsrooms in place for the trip, per the White House schedule.

This comes a Trump-appointed federal judge issued a temporary restraining against the administration banning CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House. That block is in place until 8 October, despite officials still preventing CNN from traveling on Air Force One to provide pool coverage over the weekend.

Share

Updated at 09.27 EDT

It’s also worth noting that after wrapping up its legislative agenda yesterday, the Senate is now officially on midterm recess, meaning lawmakers won’t be back on Capitol Hill until after the November elections.

Speaking to Politico, Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer projected confidence going into the final stretch of campaigning.

“We have lots of different paths to victory, and we’re not going to turn any of them down,” he told the outlet. Before they left Washington, Democrats also blocked two key Republican bills, one that attempted to introduce a way for datacenters to bear the brunt of high energy costs in their local communities, and another that would ban sitting members of Congress and their families from buying stocks in publicly traded companies.

Democrats pushed back on both pieces of legislation, saying they did not go far enough.

Share

On that note, Donald Trump will begin his day in Washington in closed-door meetings. He’ll then start his day of campaigning to Republican strongholds. First up, the president will be in Denton, Texas, where he’ll tour the Peterbilt truck manufacturing facility at 4pm ET. Then heads to Durant, Oklahoma – which sits just north of the Texas border – to give a speech at 7pm ET.

Share

Trump and Vance hit the campaign trail to support midterm candidates

President Donald Trump and vice-president JD Vance will both hit the campaign trail on Thursday, but they will be heading to heavily Republican areas to shore up lagging enthusiasm in their party ahead of next month’s midterm elections.

Trump will continue his outreach in Texas and Oklahoma today, kicking off what the president said will be a 32-day campaign blitz. Meanwhile, Vance will rally in Florida. Both events mean that the top GOP officials will be stumping in parts of the country where the party would expect glide paths to victory for their candidates – but are now facing tougher races.

Republicans have expressed growing pessimism about their chances in the election, which will determine control of Congress, as the president has repeatedly dismissed concerns about high costs and gas prices as his unpopular war in Iran drags on.

According to Trump, his party’s headwinds are merely a matter of poor public relations about a job he says is well done. “We’re not getting the word out,” he told reporters on Wednesday. “I mean, we’re just not getting it.”

Share

Updated at 08.06 EDT

David Smith

Democratic senators have accused Donald Trump’s administration of worsening the country’s childcare crisis, warning that rising costs and daycare closures are leaving families with fewer affordable options.

In a letter seen by the Guardian and addressed to Alex Adams, assistant secretary of the Administration for Children and Families (ACF), senators led by Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts argue that federal cuts and changes to childcare programs like Head Start are destabilising an already fragile system.

Childcare costs rose faster than overall inflation in 2025, the letter notes, while the cost of daycare and preschool increased by 3.5% in the year to May 2026.

“American families face skyrocketing child care costs,” the senators write, asserting that rising prices for food, supplies, insurance, rent and utilities are forcing providers to choose between increasing tuition fees and closing.

The letter says more than 400 daycare centres have closed in Oklahoma since November, while more than 300 programmes have shut in Indiana since September last year.

The senators also criticise the administration’s handling of Head Start, the federal programme providing early education and other services to low-income children.

“The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) unlawfully froze program funding for grantees mere weeks after President Trump took office – which forced some Head Start programs to temporarily close and left thousands of the country’s most vulnerable families’ child care with uncertainty – and withheld funding from grantees until they complied with the administration’s rigid requirements,” the letter says.

The letter also highlights an ACF decision in January to freeze $2.4bn in Child Care and Development Fund grants for five states. The freeze was subsequently rescinded after legal challenges, but the senators warned that a similar move could happen again.

Share

Christa Pike, convicted of murdering a classmate three decades ago, survived Tennessee’s effort to execute her by means of an unprecedented two lethal injections, prison officials said.

This was the state’s first attempted execution of a woman in 200 years. “At one point … she said, ‘my arm feels like it’s about to burst open’,” said Tori Gessner, a news anchor for ABC affiliate WKRN, who witnessed the attempted execution, before adding “then she smiles really big”.

Other journalists present described Pike snoring, exhaling loudly and gasping.

Share

Updated at 07.51 EDT

Lauren Gambino

Xavier Becerra and Steve Hilton, the candidates running to be California’s next governor, clashed Wednesday over taxes, immigration and regulating artificial intelligence in a testy debate held days before voters begin receiving their ballots in the heavily Democratic state.

Hilton, the former Fox News host endorsed by Donald Trump, used the hourlong matchup, hosted by CNN, to argue that Becerra, a former congressman who served as health and human services secretary during the Biden administration, was not actively campaigning and instead taking voters for granted.

“He wasn’t even supposed to be the candidate,” Hilton, 57, said, referring to Becerra’s unexpected success after an unusually wild primary campaign. “I just want to ask every Californian: Aren’t you tired of that?”

Becerra, 68, pitched his experience as an asset, vowing to tackle the state’s punishing cost of living crisis while being a bulwark against the Trump administration’s policies. He accused Hilton of owing loyalty to Trump – and not the state that roundly rejected the president in each of the last three presidential elections.

“If you listen closely, you can hear Donald Trump in that response,” Becerra said of Hilton’s reply to a question about regulating the development of AI.

Share

Americans are unhappy with Trump's economy and rising prices, new poll finds

Americans are deeply frustrated with president Donald Trump’s handling of the economy and rising prices, with most panning his performance and blaming his policies as higher costs threaten his party’s chances in November.

A new poll from the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research finds that only 17% of US adults approve of the Republican president’s handling of the cost of living. Just 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, marking a new low.

A majority, 65%, of US adults now blame Trump’s policies for persistently high costs more than factors outside of his control, signaling growing weariness over his aggressive use of tariffs and continued unhappiness with the war with Iran.

The dismal numbers come just weeks before midterm elections that will determine whether Republicans maintain control of Congress and while Trump is hitting the campaign trail with an aggressive schedule of rallies.

But Trump - who has asked voters to pretend that he is on the ballot as he tries to bolster turnout - remains deeply unpopular, with even many Republicans faulting him for failing to deliver on promised relief.

Share

Updated at 07.50 EDT

Trump officials abandon effort to investigate election threats, experts warn

George Chidi

The Trump administration has abandoned key security bodies meant to investigate direct threats to US elections by foreign actors and domestic terrorists, according to former officials and a recent report.

While administration officials have been actively focused on unsubstantiated claims of widespread voter fraud by noncitizens, other credible election threats appear to have been overlooked, the officials say.

Between 2021 and 2024, the justice department’s election threats taskforce prosecuted 21 cases, like that of Solomon Peña, a failed candidate for the New Mexico house of representatives who organized shootings at the houses of election officials, or Quintez Brown, who shot up a campaign meeting of Louisville’s mayor.

Democrats and Republicans faced prosecution for harassing, intimidating and threatening elections workers, noted Nikki Fisher, former chief election security officer for the Oregon secretary of state, now the executive director of the Oregon District Attorneys Association.

Since then, the taskforce seems to have gone quiet.

“While officials are being trained to handle threats, the federal deterrent meant to punish the people making them appears to have gone quiet,” Fisher said. “To date, no new cases have been prosecuted, and the DoJ’s election threats taskforce appears to be defunct in practice.”

Share

Tennessee governor halts executions after second botched lethal injection attempt this year

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Tennessee governor Bill Lee has halted the state’s remaining executions for the rest of the year after officials were unable to put Christa Gail Pike to death yesterday.

Pike, 50, was alive and loudly snoring after the attempted lethal injection and taken by ambulance from the prison, her attorneys said. She was being treated at a hospital, but they said they hadn’t been told about her condition.

She had been scheduled for execution at 10am on Wednesday for the killing she committed at age 18 and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.

Governor Lee said that he was halting the one remaining execution for the rest of 2026 and ordered a “comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred.”

“Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the State’s most serious responsibilities, and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective,” Lee said in a statement.

The Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement that they “followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office.”

Officials gave Pike two doses of pentobarbital, her attorneys said in court filings late Wednesday. The state’s execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered “if the inmate is not deceased” after the first set. It does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set.

It was the second time this year that Tennessee has been unable to carry out an execution. In May, state officials called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and killing three people in 1994, after executioners tried and failed for over an hour to place an IV to administer pentobarbital.

In other developments:

The latest in a series of pro-Trump ads the Trump administration is using taxpayer funds to air on television in the run-up to the the midterm elections is a 1-minute spot that celebrates his decision to go to war with Iran.

Pete Hegseth announced that Elon Musk will co-lead a government project to study the future of warfare, with Palmer Luckey, CEO of the defense tech company Anduril, and Newt Gingrich, the former Republican speaker of the House.

An internal watchdog said the Federal Reserve mismanaged costs associated with a $2.4bn renovation of its Washington DC headquarters, but noted that no criminal violations occurred, according to a report released Wednesday.

Trump said South Korea plans to invest about $54bn in a natural gas project in Alaska.

Xavier Becerra and Steve Hilton, the candidates running to be California’s next governor, clashed Wednesday over taxes, immigration and regulating artificial intelligence in a testy debate held days before voters begin receiving their ballots in the heavily Democratic state.

text:
The family of Renee Good, the woman killed by immigration agents in January in Minneapolis, filed two federal lawsuits against the agent who shot her and several top officials in the Trump administration on Thursday.

In the lawsuits, Good’s partner, Becca Good, and her brother, Brent Ganger, alleged wrongful death and other violations of federal law, according to a press release issued by their lawyers.

Good was a US citizen and mother of three who, on 7 January, joined her wife in protesting against the deployment of thousands of ICE agents in their city as part of the Trump administration’s mass deportation policy.

The 37-year-old woman was shot and killed in her car by an agent who claimed he acted in self-defense, and the Department of Homeland Security claimed that she had engaged in “an act of domestic terrorism”. Multiple video clips of the encounter, however, show that Good was steering her vehicle away from the agent as she tried to drive away.

Her death and that of Alex Pretti, an American nurse who was also shot and killed by an immigration agent during Minneapolis protests two weeks later, sparked outrage and a wave of anger across the country.

Shortly after Good’s killing, Todd Blanche, then the deputy US attorney general, said he saw no grounds for opening a civil rights investigation. Days later, the justice department opened an investigation into the relationship between Becca Good, the deceased’s partner, and protest groups. At least 10 prosecutors resigned following the fatal shootings.

Now these lawsuits have become some of the first major civil litigation actions filed against Trump’s deportation campaign in Minnesota.

In one of them, the attorneys for Good’s wife and brother allege wrongful death and seek to recover – receive damages – for the “immense suffering Renee endured in the final moments of her life and for the profound and permanent losses that her death has inflicted upon her family”.

“The complaint also seeks to recover for Becca Good, who was standing feet from the couple’s vehicle when Ross fired three rounds into it, and she watched her partner die,” the complaint says.

“Peaceful assembly, speech and even dissent are protected rights. However, the government has distorted the exercise of these rights as violence against our republic and acted with extreme and unconstitutional force, causing egregious harm. Many of these illegal uses of force resulted in death – including the death of an American mother of three, Renee Good … Today’s legal actions demand accountability for countless violations of the law, the constitution and the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) own rules governing the use of force,” the lawsuit says.

The other lawsuit alleges a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights by senior federal officials and federal immigration enforcement agents, and names Jonathan Ross, the immigration officer who shot Good, the former homeland security secretary Kristi Noem, the White House deputy chief of staff and architect of hardline US immigration policies, Stephen Miller, and former US border patrol officer Gregory Bovino, among others, for their “roles in Renee Good’s death”.

text:
The family of a woman who was killed by an immigration agent in Minneapolis in January has announced two lawsuits against the US government and members of the Trump administration.

Renee Good, a US citizen, was shot to death by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer during a major immigration sweep. Millions watched the video recorded of her killing and residents of the Minnesota city took to the streets to protest.

One lawsuit blames the government for her death, claiming the operation created "an unprecedented environment for state-sponsored violence", a lawyer for the family said.

Speaking publicly for the first time since the shooting, Becca Good told a news conference on the lawsuits on Thursday: "The whole world had to watch as our entire universe was destroyed."

"We were all robbed," she said as she described how the shooting affected their three children.

In one of the lawsuits, the family accuses the government of "battery, assault, false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligence that caused Renee's death".

It cites the Federal Tort Claims Act, which allows citizens to sue the government for personal injury, death, or property damage caused by the negligence of federal employees.

The second lawsuit targets ICE officer Jonathan Ross, who shot Good, as well as White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, White House border chief Tom Homan and others, alleging a "conspiracy to interfere with civil rights by senior federal officials, federal immigration enforcement agents, and private actors".

"Our government has become a grave and mortal threat to its own citizens," the family's lawyer, Antonio Romanucci said at the news conference.

Trump initially blamed Good's own actions for her death, saying just hours after she was killed that she "violently, willfully, and viciously ran over the ICE officer". Weeks later, he called her death a "tragedy" and said agents sometimes are "going to make a mistake".

Good was a 37-year-old mother of three who had just moved to the city. She was shot on 7 January in a traffic stop, which immigration authorities said occurred after she made "an attempt to kill or cause bodily harm to agents". Witnesses disputed that she was attempting to attack officers.

Weeks later, hundreds of federal agents were withdrawn from the city and the official in charge of the operation, Greg Bovino, was removed from his post.

At least 10 people have been killed in encounters with immigration officers during Trump's second term, which began in January 2025, according to the Associated Press news agency.

On Tuesday, Good's mother testified in a congressional hearing, saying: "I am a registered Republican. I voted for President Trump under the impression that these agents were here to protect the citizens of the United States."

text:
AUSTIN, Texas — A Venezuelan delivery driver who was shot in his car by a federal immigration agent in Texas will remain in custody on charges that he assaulted an officer while trying to evade arrest, a federal judge ruled Wednesday.

Judge Dustin Howell said that the case against Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, should proceed after prosecutors presented body-worn camera footage of the encounter in Austin, in which Garcés Pérez allegedly struck a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer with his driver’s side mirror.

Garcés Pérez is charged with one count of assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer and faces up to 20 years in prison if convicted. His case has sparked widespread outrage across the Texas capital city and brought renewed criticism from Democrats of President Donald Trump’s aggressive crackdown on immigration.

With a bullet still lodged in his back, Garcés Pérez appeared in court in a wheelchair. His attorneys said he still urgently needs medical care, 10 days after being shot. He also wore a sling on his arm and needed help putting on a headset to listen to a translation of the proceedings.

The defense called the charges against Garcés Pérez “retaliation” and argued that the camera footage was inconclusive because it didn’t fully capture the moment when he allegedly tried to flee.

The hearing also included testimony from Homeland Security Investigations Special Agent Rick Bazan, who signed the criminal complaint charging Garcés Pérez with assault. The defense argued that Bazan, whose agency is the investigative arm of ICE, could not confirm whether the ICE agent was actually hit by the car mirror since no federal investigators interviewed the agent directly. Bazan also couldn’t explain why the officer allegedly struck by the mirror was not wearing a body-worn camera.

Footage provided Wednesday in court shows officers pulling Garcés Pérez over Sept. 20 in Austin, where he was making deliveries for DoorDash.

The video showed Garcés Pérez giving officers his drivers license through a crack in his window and then asking in Spanish if he can park his car so that a relative could come retrieve it. The officer demanded Garcés Pérez get out of the car multiple times, to which he asked if he could park his own car so a family member could come retrieve it. After a back and forth, Garcés Pérez abruptly and rapidly drives off.

Prosecutors show video but not of the shooting itself

Prosecutors presented a video from cameras at a nearby business showing the ensuing high-speed chase through residential streets. The shooting itself was not captured on the footage shared in court.

The federal officer who shot Garcés Pérez wasn’t wearing a body-worn camera. The immigration officer who did have a camera was driving in a separate car and turned the camera off during the pursuit.

Garcés Pérez said he was struck by a law enforcement SUV and spun around before he was shot. Federal officers told investigators, however, that Garcés Pérez attempted to strike an officer with his car at the end of the chase before the unidentified officer fired his weapon.

The accusations against Garcés Pérez recall previous claims made by immigration agents after other high-profile shootings similarly accusing drivers of weaponizing their vehicles. In a handful of cases, the allegations have been undermined or walked back after the release of body-worn camera footage, drawing renewed scrutiny about the DHS’s reliance on vehicular stops to execute arrests.

Lawyer accuses ICE of denying him medical treatment

Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, one of Garcés Pérez’s immigration attorneys, accused ICE of denying him medical treatment for his bullet wound.

“ICE’s conduct has been so egregious, that physicians, nurses, medical ethicists and health advocates have come together to demand his release,” she said outside court after the hearing.

Garcés Pérez entered the U.S. in 2024 using CBP One, a program begun under President Joe Biden that allowed migrants to schdule appointments with U.S. authorities to be considered for asylum. President Donald Trump ended the program on his first day back in office.

Garcés Pérez was an asylum seeker and had a valid work permit, according to his lawyer. She said a judge later issued a deportation order after Garcés Pérez missed an immigration court hearing because the notice had been sent to a former address.

Judge Howell said he denied Garcés Pérez bond on the basis that he could be a flight risk to Venezuela, where he has a child.

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers will only be allowed to conduct vehicle stops if they have completed related training courses and must ensure that vehicles used for stops are equipped with lights and sirens, according to new internal guidance reviewed by CNN.

The guidance comes on the heels of multiple controversial vehicle stops that have resulted in fatal, and non-fatal, shootings and against the backdrop of internal tension within the Trump administration over how to proceed with the stops, which the administration considers a key tool as it ramps up immigration arrests.

According to the guidance, only Enforcement and Removal Operations officers, who have “successfully completed” one of six agency training courses, can conduct “traditional vehicle stops, and call-back vehicle stops commonly known as high-risk or felony vehicle stops.”

Those who have not completed one of those courses can only participate in a support capacity.

The guidance states that all officers on scene “must have an agency-issued and activated body worn camera.” It also states that “under no circumstances” are officers authorized to engage in vehicle pursuits in instances where people fail to pull over, but instead to take down information for further investigation.

CNN reached out to the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement for comment.

Earlier this summer, Trump was furious over a pause on most vehicle stops conducted by ICE following fatal shootings in Texas and Maine. The decision to pause those stops, which Trump ultimately overturned, immediately received pushback from his political base, who believed it was a sign of the administration going soft on its immigration crackdown.

The new guidance doesn’t prohibit vehicle stops but lays out who is allowed to participate — and in what capacity — and how to perform them.

The guidance, for example, also weighs in on vehicle stops that involve the pinning of a vehicle and use of tire deflation devices. It describes pinning as using a vehicle or physical barrier to trap or stop a car.

Officers are permitted to pin a vehicle “for the safety of the suspected vehicle and its occupants, the ICE officers engaged in vehicle stops, and other motorists on the roadway.”

Throughout Trump’s second term, vehicle stops have been at the center of several interactions between federal officers and immigrants they are trying to detain, as well as US citizens. Several crashes involving fleeing suspects or protesters accused of “ramming” federal officers have been caught on video.

Earlier this year, a US citizen, Renee Good was fatally shot by an ICE officer in Minneapolis while driving her car and protesting ICE officers. The Department of Homeland Security initially said Good tried to weaponize her vehicle against the officer, but video and witness accounts called into question DHS’ version of events. Good’s family filed two civil lawsuits related to her death on Thursday.

In July, two immigrants, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston and Joan Sebastian Durán Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine, were fatally shot by ICE officers in separate incidents about a week apart. Those shootings and their fallout prompted DHS to direct ICE officers to briefly suspend most vehicle stops and coordinate more closely with local agencies when executing a criminal warrant on someone inside a vehicle.

And last month, an ICE officer shot and wounded a man from Venezuela who was working as a DoorDash driver in Austin, Texas.

This story has been updated with additional information.

description:

We call on the authorities to close the facility and end the detention of children and families at this site.
Close the detention facility operating at England Airpark.
An existing facility with a record of concerns The proposed facility would expand an existing deportation hub at England Airpark.
Concerns about children’s rights and due process The proposed facility also raises concerns about the legal protections available to children.
text:
An agreement with US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has led to the opening of a child and family detention facility at an airpark in Alexandria, Louisiana. The facility has a capacity of 528 beds and detains children and families on one of the most polluted sites in the United States. Contamination levels at the site are reportedly 5,000 times higher than recommended limits.

By detaining children and families in these conditions, authorities expose them to serious health risks. The facility not only detains and deports children and families but also subjects them to potentially harmful environmental conditions. We call on the authorities to close the facility and end the detention of children and families at this site.

Here’s what you can do:

Write to the Executive Director of England Air Park Board of Commissioners urging him to:

End England Airpark’s collaboration with US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Cancel the contract with the LaSalle Family Foundation.

Close the detention facility operating at England Airpark.

Write to:

Minister of Justice

Alfred Ahingejeje

1880 – Bujumbura, Burundi

Email: info@justice.gov.bi

X: @MiniJusticeBdi

Salutation: Dear Director Hennessy,

And copy:

His Excellency Peter Hoekstra

Ambassador

Embassy of the United States of America

490 Sussex Drive

Ottawa, ON K1N 1G8

Tel: (613) 238-5335 / 688-5335 (24h) Fax: (613) 688-3082

Plans for a new child and family detention facility

England Airpark in Alexandria, Louisiana, is a former military air base that now houses Alexandria International Airport. In February 2026, the England Airpark Board of Commissioners entered into a five-year contract to convert former Air Force barracks into a staging facility for children and families.

The proposed facility would have a capacity of 528 beds. Authorities intend to use it for short-term detention before deporting children and families directly from the adjoining airpark. However, under the Trump administration, families have increasingly faced extended detention. Some families with children have reportedly been detained for several months or even over a year.

An existing facility with a record of concerns

The proposed facility would expand an existing deportation hub at England Airpark. In June 2025, as deportation flights reached a five-year high, Alexandria ranked first among the country’s busiest deportation hubs. The airport averaged 14 deportation flights per day throughout 2025.

The existing facility also has a documented pattern of health emergencies and due process violations. Of the approximately 28,000 people detained there, roughly 20% were held for longer than the 72-hour limit.

Serious environmental and health risks

The proposed facility sits on a former military base with significant environmental contamination. The ground contains high concentrations of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), which are persistent chemicals linked to health risks. PFAS concentrations in the ground are reportedly around 575,000 times the federal limit for groundwater.

The site also contains trichloroethylene (TCE), a contaminant linked to serious health conditions, including cancer and liver damage. Detaining children and families at this site could expose them to additional health risks.

The American Academy of Pediatrics has found that even brief detention can have long-term consequences for children. These include post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety, depression and suicidal ideation.

Concerns about children’s rights and due process

The proposed facility also raises concerns about the legal protections available to children. In the United States, the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) takes custody of unaccompanied children. However, ORR is not involved in the current plan. Instead, the children would be placed in the custody of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

This change in custody raises concerns because strict federal guidelines protect children in ORR care. Children held by ICE outside the usual process may not receive the same legal protections against forced removal from the country.

ICE is also already in violation of the Flores Settlement Agreement. This 1997 consent decree sets minimum standards for the treatment, placement and release of children in US immigration custody. The proposed facility raises further concerns about the treatment of children and respect for their rights.

text:
The family and partner of Renee Good, the 37-year-old mother killed by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in Minneapolis, filed lawsuits Wednesday against the federal government and President Trump for damages following the shooting.

Good was fatally shot on Jan. 7 during the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) immigration crackdown in Minnesota called Operation Metro Surge.

One of the lawsuits — which named former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, other Trump administration officials and the officers involved in the shooting — said the operation was “designed to be a violent and discriminatory campaign targeted at Minnesotans on the basis of race and national origin.”

“Renee was one of those casualties,” the lawyers for Good’s family continued.

The other lawsuit named the “United States of America” as the defendant, which allows Good’s next of kin to sue the federal government for personal injury.

This complaint cited the Hennepin County medical examiner who ruled Good’s death as a homicide following a private autopsy and the office finding “three clear gunshot wound paths” to her body.

“Each of Ross’s three shots was fired in violation” of DHS mandatory policy, which permits officers to use force only when “no reasonably effective, safe, and feasible alternative appears to exist,” the lawyers for Good’s partner, Becca Good, wrote, referencing one of the officers, Jonathan Ross.

Video from bystanders showed an officer approaching an SUV stopped across the middle of the road, demanding Good open the door before he grabbed the handle of the vehicle.

Good’s vehicle begins to pull forward and a different ICE officer standing in front of the vehicle pulls his weapon and immediately fires multiple shots into the vehicle at close range, jumping back as the vehicle moves toward him. The SUV then sped into two cars parked on a curb nearby before crashing to a stop.

The lawsuit alleged Ross, the officer who shot and killed Good, also shouted obscenities at the woman while she pulled forward, yelling “f‑‑‑ing b‑‑‑‑.”

Video appeared to show Good’s neighbor, a doctor, being told to step back after he offered medical care for her twice.

Her death, and another shooting involving the killing of 37-year-old Alex Pretti by an ICE officer in Minneapolis a week later, sparked waves of intense protests across the state.

ICE and DHS did not respond immediately to The Hill’s request for comment.

text:
October 1, 2026 11:00 am

Media Contact

125 Broad Street

18th Floor

New York, NY 10004

United States

WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court today agreed to hear argument this term in Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, stemming from a lawsuit brought by the American Civil Liberties Union, New York Civil Liberties Union, and the Law Office of Paul Dwyer PC challenging the Trump administration’s new policy subjecting millions of immigrants to mandatory detention without access to bond hearings.

In July 2025, the Trump administration suddenly adopted a new radical misinterpretation of immigration law, declaring that anyone who entered without inspection must be detained without access to bond or due process regardless of how long that person has lived in the country or their ties to family and community.

Hundreds of federal district judges have ruled on thousands of related habeas petitions, with nine out of 10 judges ruling that the administration’s misinterpretation of immigration law is illegal. Nine federal appeals courts have also ruled against the policy, including a Second Circuit ruling at the center of this case.

The following is reaction to the Supreme Court’s decision to hear the case:

“The courts have repeatedly and resoundingly rejected the Trump administration’s radical misinterpretation of the law. Try as it might, the government cannot twist the law to detain immigrants for months or even years on end without a bond hearing. Not only is it cruel and inhumane; it is unlawful. We look forward to making that case to the Supreme Court,” said Michael K.T. Tan, deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project.

“The Trump administration’s policy of detaining immigrants without any process is both inhumane and unlawful,” said Amy Belsher, director of Immigrants’ Rights Litigation at the New York Civil Liberties Union. “Despite their best efforts, the government cannot rewrite the law to detain millions of noncitizens, many of whom have lived here for decades, without an opportunity to seek release. The Immigration and Nationality Act, and fundamental fairness, require the government to, at a minimum, allow people to make a case for their release. We look forward to making that clear to the Supreme Court."

“Mr. Barbosa da Cunha has been living in the U.S. for the last 22 years. He is a hard-working, small-business owner, with a U.S. citizen family and no criminal history. He has never missed an immigration appointment or hearing. Detaining him without the possibility of release on bond serves no purpose other than to punish him for being an immigrant, and has been solidly rejected by every court to have considered his case. We are confident that the Supreme Court will agree," said attorney Paul Dwyer of the Law Office of Paul Dwyer PC.

text:
The family of Renee Good filed two federal civil lawsuits Thursday against the U.S. government and several top federal officials over Good's fatal shooting by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent in Minneapolis earlier this year.

The lawsuits were filed nearly ten months after Good, a Minneapolis mother of three, was in the driver's seat of her Honda Pilot in the middle of a residential street when an ICE agent opened fire. Federal officials say the agent acted in self defense after Good tried to ram him with her car.

"What happened to her is completely senseless," Good's brother Brent Ganger told reporters after the suit was filed. "The time is absolutely now for accountability. We will not be quiet. We will not go away."

"The day of accountability has arrived for the United States' rogue agencies, Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection, and the unjustified and excessive use of force -- let alone deadly force -- used on people exercising their rights under the Constitution's Bill of Rights," Good's legal team said in a statement.

One of the complaints, filed under the Federal Tort Claims Act for wrongful death against the U.S. government, alleges that federal law enforcement officers used excessive and deadly force against Good.

The second complaint was filed against top officials including White House senior adviser Stephen Miller, former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, Border Czar Tom Homan, and ICE agent Jonathan Ross, who fired the fatal shots, as well as other federal agents.

"What happened to us should never happen to any family. No child should grow up without a parent. No one should lose their sister or their daughter," Renee's partner, Becca Good, said following the filing of the suit.

Antonio M. Romanucci, an attorney for the family, said the suits were filed because they have not heard back from the federal government regarding the shooting.

"We have heard nothing, we know nothing, period," Romanucci said, adding that Ross is the person who "deserves an investigation."

"There was only one person who pulled the trigger on Jan. 7, and that's the person who deserves the investigation," he said.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment from ABC News.

The complaint alleges that top officials engaged in a "carefully planned, coordinated effort between senior federal officials and private actors to make two ethnic communities in Minnesota -- Minnesotans of Somali and Hispanic descent and origin -- the object of aggression and abduction."

According to the complaint, Ross fired through Good's windshield and open driver-side window as her SUV was turning away from him. The filing states that Ross stepped toward the car, fired a round through the windshield, and then fired twice more through her open window as the vehicle completed a turn.

"The operation was in essence the domestic deployment of a paramilitary force of three to four thousand masked, armed, camouflaged agents, outfitted in military tactical gear including camouflage, helmets, gas masks, and military-grade weapons, wielding instruments of war to carry out domestic shock-and-awe tactics to intimidate the populace" the complaint states.
