text:
Last week, the Trump administration moved to cancel millions of dollars in funding for programs for illegal aliens and foreign nationals as part of an $810 million pocket rescission. The rescission cancellation is the administration’s latest effort to combat illegal immigration and put American citizens first.

According to a White House memo published Friday, cutting these programs will provide savings to Americans, help further eliminate wasteful spending, and rather than welcoming illegal aliens, ensure they are being held accountable. Of the $810 million recission, funding designated specifically for anti-borders programs and grants included:

$567 million from Health and Human Services (HHS) for nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) with programs facilitating illegal immigration and exploiting unaccompanied children

$70 million for institutions importing foreign students and faculty to the United States

$50 million from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Department of Education (DOE) providing legal aid for illegal aliens and teaching encouraging foreign nationals to take advantage of our education system and avoid law enforcement

The administration’s move takes strides towards easing the financial burden of illegal immigration on American taxpayers, which FAIR estimates to be at least $150.7 billion annually. While some appropriators in Congress have pushed back, and the Government Accountability Office (GAO) is set to issue a report against the practice, Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Director Russ Vought indicated the administration is moving ahead. He described the rescission as “an attempt to get at the border industrial complex, which furthered illegal immigration. It is another aspect of shutting off the number of people that can come into the system… and then getting at the funding source.”

FAIR looks forward to continued work with Congress and the White House to ensure illegal immigration is never rewarded, nor foreign nationals baselessly offered services at the expense of American taxpayers.

text:
Thirty years ago, President Bill CIinton signed the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRIRA) and the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 (AEDPA) into law, creating legal tools that have allowed President Donald Trump’s administration to quickly implement its agenda of mass detention and deportation. Together, these laws immediately increased the number of people who were subject to deportation and detention and vastly expanded the overlap between the criminal and immigration systems. Over time, IIRIRA and AEDPA built the foundation for the immigration system the United States has today—one that strips immigrants of due process, criminalizes them, and continues to expand detention.

Supercharged by two rounds of federal reconciliation funding in which Congress bypassed the annual appropriations process to award a total of $240 billion for immigration enforcement, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) have more money than ever, magnifying the harms of the 1996 laws to devastating effect. Worse yet, lawmakers continue their attempts to double down on IIRIRA’s approach by introducing a slate of bills that would further gut due process and impose severe consequences in people’s immigration cases. If we are to build an immigration system that prioritizes human dignity and due process over humiliation and punishment, we must first understand the policies that laid the groundwork for the Trump administration’s agenda today.

Expedited removal: How the Trump administration is bypassing immigration due process

In its efforts to deport as many people as quickly as possible, the Trump administration has relied heavily on expedited removal, a fast-tracked deportation mechanism created by IIRIRA that bypasses typical immigration proceedings. People placed in this category do not get a hearing with a judge. Instead, immigration officers decide if a person’s detention and deportation are lawful. Past administrations primarily applied expedited removal for people who were encountered by immigration enforcement within 100 miles of a U.S. land border and who had been in the country for less than two weeks. But the first and second Trump administrations expanded the use of expedited removal nationwide and increased the time threshold to two years.

People placed into expedited removal are often deported within a single day, making it virtually impossible to consult with an attorney or gather evidence. Trump’s expansion of expedited removal has been challenged by advocates in court who have raised due process concerns, but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit recently sided with the administration, citing IIRIRA more than 20 times in its decision.

Mandatory detention: Depriving people of liberty without due process

IIRIRA didn’t just make deporting people easier. It also made the act of detaining people without bond hearings—called mandatory detention—commonplace. A bond hearing gives people the chance to be released while their immigration case proceeds, which in turn enables them to prepare for hearings, meet with a lawyer, and remain in their community while they wait for their time in court. IIRIRA vastly expanded mandatory detention by requiring the detention of noncitizens who are “applicants for admission” into the country. This practice has largely meant that asylum seekers presenting themselves to immigration officers at the border or ports of entry have been placed in mandatory detention with no opportunity to see a judge to request release on bond.

In July 2025, the Department of Homeland Security issued a memo stating that it would now consider anyone who entered the country without inspection as an “applicant for admission,” effectively ending bond hearings for many undocumented people, regardless of how long they have been living in the country. In response, attorneys filed tens of thousands of habeas corpus petitions in federal court to challenge their clients’ detention. This year, by early August, more than 11,800 people had been released from detention as a result of a federal court order, nearly 10 times the number during the same period in 2025. Nine federal appeals courts have rejected the administration’s mandatory detention policy, resulting in a circuit court split on the issue that could prompt U.S. Supreme Court review. In the meantime, some undocumented immigrants are being granted bond hearings while others are not, depending on which circuit court has jurisdiction over their cases.

The Trump administration did not need the Supreme Court, however, to expand mandatory detention. In January 2025, President Trump signed the Laken Riley Act, a bipartisan law that broadened the criteria for mandatory detention. For the first time, the law empowers ICE to detain people without bond hearings based on arrests, charges, or even allegations involving certain theft-related crimes, without requiring a conviction. The Laken Riley Act builds on the framework established by IIRIRA and AEDPA, further tying immigration detention to the criminal justice system.

The myth of immigrant criminality and its harms

Falsely connecting immigrants with crime has roots in the country’s early racial exclusion laws, and this harmful narrative continues to drive policies that entangle the immigration system with the criminal justice system. Congress created the “aggravated felony” category for immigration law purposes through the Anti–Drug Abuse Act of 1988 to cover three offenses: murder, drug trafficking, and firearm trafficking. Congress has since added other offenses to the list, but the most substantial changes were implemented through AEDPA and IIRIRA in 1996. These laws widened the category considerably to add nonviolent offenses—and even some crimes classified by states as misdemeanors. The term is thus misleading: an offense need not be aggravated or classified as a felony under state law to trigger serious immigration consequences.

People deemed to have committed an aggravated felony under these immigration laws are not only subject to mandatory detention but also, in some cases, expedited removal and a lifetime ban on legally returning to the United States if deported. These severe immigration consequences further compound the disproportionately harmful outcomes for Black and Latino immigrants that already exist in the criminal justice system due to racial bias. Compared to non-Black immigrants, for example, Black immigrants are detained for longer periods, are more likely to be placed in solitary confinement, and are subject to higher rates of violence and abuse in detention.

text:
On 3 September 2026 the Home Office published its Autumn Immigration Rules update. Key changes include new protections for Skilled Worker visa holders who are victims of modern slavery, measures to prevent abuse of fee waiver and biometrics processes, and updates to support the UK rejoining Erasmus+ from January 2027. There are also some useful expansions of permitted visitor route activities for those receiving training or coming to the UK for creative purposes.

Further details of the changes are outlined below, including when they come into effect.

Changes to Appendix Skilled Worker to support victims of modern slavery

Skilled Worker visa holders are not normally permitted to take up other work if they are not continuing to work in the job they are sponsored to do. However, from 8 October 2026 this restriction may be lifted for any Skilled Worker who has been recognised as a victim of modern slavery.

The liberalisation of work conditions will be restricted to those who have received a positive Conclusive Grounds decision via the National Referral Mechanism.

Details of how the process will work in practice are yet to be released by the Home Office, but once notified of the change to their immigration conditions, an individual will be allowed to work with minimal restrictions (including undertaking self-employment and voluntary work) for the rest of their existing Skilled Worker visa. The remaining restriction is that they will not be allowed to work as a professional sportsperson or sports coach. There will be no change to the immigration restriction prohibiting a Skilled Worker from accessing prescribed public funds.

This change, combined with the recently published temporary arrangement confirming the Home Office won't curtail the immigration permission of adult social care workers following sponsor licence revocation, could mean that victims have greater incentive to come forward and report modern slavery.

The Government is also taking other measures to combat worker exploitation. Earlier this month, the Government named nearly 660 employers who failed to pay staff the National Minimum Wage, returning £4 million directly to workers.

The Home Office is also continuing to consider the sponsorship system reforms indicated in last year's immigration white paper. Any reforms in this area will aim to put more responsibility and accountability on effective and responsible sponsors. Potentially the revised system may reduce the risk of worker exploitation by making it easier for work route visa holders to move between licensed sponsors throughout the duration of their visa.

Change to when a fee waiver extends immigration permission

A change is made to para 34G(4) of the Immigration Rules. This confirms that when a fee waiver application has been made, the date of the subsequent immigration application will only be the date of the fee waiver request if the immigration application is the human rights application connected to the fee waiver request.

The change is in place for immigration applications made on or after 8 October 2026.

The amendment is aimed at preventing the exploitation of the fee waiver process by applicants who use the fee waiver process to access a statutory extension of their immigration permission ahead of submitting a non-human rights application.

One consequence of this change is that some potential work route applicants may need to make an application for entry clearance rather than seeking to extend their permission in-country as an overstayer. The options in each case should be assessed on a case-by-case basis.

Varying immigration applications – single period to enrol biometrics

Where an application is made on or after 8 October 2026 to vary an outstanding application, the biometrics must still be enrolled by the deadline applicable to the previous application. In essence, there will only be a single period to enrol biometrics.

Again, this change is targeted at preventing abuse by applicants who aim to prolong a statutory extension of their permission by making an application and then varying it multiple times without enrolling their biometrics. This has been effective in the past because an application can't be substantively considered until the validity requirements for it (including biometric enrolment) have been met.

Changes relating to the UK rejoining the Erasmus+ programme

The UK has agreed with the EU to rejoin the Erasmus+ programme for education, training, youth and sport from 1 January 2027.

For applications made on or after 8 October 2026, the following changes are made to facilitate immigration processes relating to this development:

Appendix Government Authorised Exchange schemes is updated to add the 'Erasmus+' scheme on the same basis as other scheme requirements and conditions;

Appendix V is updated to permit visitors participating in an Erasmus+ project to study at UK state funded schools and academies for up to 6 months, subject to child safeguarding and other eligibility requirements being met;

Appendix Student is amended to enable students undertaking a course as part of the Erasmus+ programme to be sponsored regardless of whether the course of study leads to an approved qualification;

A new category of permitted activities for visitors entitled 'Erasmus+ activities' has been added, enabling Erasmus+ participants to carry out specific programme-related training, education and work experience activities.

The permitted activities for visitors are expanded as mentioned in the section below.

Changes to permitted activities for visitors

The changes below apply to those who make an application for a visitor visa or for entry as a visitor on or after 8 October 2026.

Participation in workshops, debates and Skills Competitions

Partly to further facilitate participation in Erasmus+, all visitors (including those not participating in Erasmus+) will be allowed to participate in workshops and debates, and to attend Skills Competitions.

Receiving training in the UK

When visitors come to the UK to undertake training, they will no longer have to show that this training is unavailable in their home country.

Attending rehearsals for visiting artists, entertainers and musicians

Visitors who are artists, entertainers, and musicians will be permitted to attend rehearsals in addition to performances.

Permitted activities for entertainment staff

A new definition of 'entertainment staff' is introduced for visitor route purposes, meaning an individual employed by an organisation, entertainer, musician, or artist to support in the preparation, setting up and running of an event held within the UK.

Entertainment staff may support a visiting artist, entertainer or musician provided they are employed by that person outside the UK and are assisting them in connection with the same permitted creative activities their employer is coming to the UK to participate in.

Changes to refusal grounds – frustrating immigration controls

With effect from 8 October 2026, a change to Part Suitability confirms that if an applicant has previously acted to frustrate immigration controls (e.g. by failing to report for bail or absconding from bail or custody), they will be classed as having been in breach of immigration laws when making an in-country application for permission to stay.

The amendment aligns in-country refusal grounds with those for entry clearance.

title: ICE is detaining pregnant immigrants. Most Americans say they shouldn't. - The 19th News
description:
More than half of Black and Hispanic Americans say they should never be held in immigration detention.
Even among Republicans, only 30 percent said they support a general policy of detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing immigrants.
The 19th has been reporting on Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) detentions of pregnant, nursing and postpartum immigrants since President Donald Trump’s second inauguration.

text:
More than two-thirds of Americans say that immigrants who are pregnant, nursing or have recently given birth should generally not be held in immigration detention, according to a new 19th News/YouGov poll.

The Trump administration’s immigration crackdown has led to more arrests, detentions and deportations of pregnant and postpartum immigrants, who are more medically vulnerable than the general population. About 29 percent of respondents said that immigrants who are pregnant, have recently given birth or are nursing should be detained only in “exceptional circumstances,” and 41 percent said they should not be kept in detention facilities at all.

Women are more likely to oppose the policy.

Only 12 percent of women believe that immigrants facing deportation should be held in detention even if they are pregnant, postpartum or nursing a baby, compared with 72 percent who say this group never should be or should be only in exceptional circumstances.

Men are overall more likely to support the detention of pregnant, postpartum and nursing immigrants, but still, most men — 68 percent — say they should not be held or be held only in exceptional circumstances.

Overall, Americans don’t agree with the administration’s approach.

There’s no demographic subset of Americans polled that says immigrants facing deportation should, as a rule, be held in detention even if they are pregnant, postpartum or nursing a baby. More than half of Black and Hispanic Americans say they should never be held in immigration detention.

Even among Republicans, only 30 percent said they support a general policy of detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing immigrants. Meanwhile, 55 percent either said these people should not be detained or should be detained only in exceptional circumstances.

The poll also showed that most Democrats and Independents — 85 percent and 57 percent, respectively — believe the Trump administration is doing “too much” when it comes to deporting immigrants. A majority of women, 55 percent, also said they believe the administration is doing “too much,” compared with 45 percent of men surveyed.

Here’s why we asked.

The 19th has been reporting on Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) detentions of pregnant, nursing and postpartum immigrants since President Donald Trump’s second inauguration. In March, the Department of Homeland Security confirmed that 363 pregnant, postpartum and nursing immigrants were deported between January 1, 2025, and February 16, 2026, out of 498 who were detained and then left an ICE facility during that time, either via deportation or release.

A Biden-era policy directed ICE not to detain, arrest or take into custody pregnant, postpartum or breastfeeding people simply for breaking immigration laws, except under “exceptional circumstances.” The Trump administration has not formally reversed that policy, but reports from across the country confirm that ICE has detained numerous pregnant immigrants since Trump took office.

The Department of Homeland Security has said it detains these immigrants infrequently and that those who are detained receive “comprehensive medical care.”

Over the last 18 months, The 19th has spoken with several women who say that they were detained despite having no criminal record or having only traffic violations. Several had pending asylum applications.

Many of them shared that they did not receive basic healthcare — including breast pumps, prenatal visits, vitamins or extra food — while detained. Nayra Guzmán, said she did not have a bed to sleep on, despite being in recovery for a recent Cesarean section. Amanda Isabel Fanego Cardoso said she was diagnosed with preeclampsia and gestational diabetes after being released but was not made aware of those conditions while in detention.

Americans broadly support access to pregnancy-related healthcare for detained immigrants.

If pregnant, postpartum or nursing immigrants are detained, the poll found, Americans broadly believe those people should be given basic pregnancy-related healthcare. About two-thirds of respondents — 67 percent — said these immigrants should be given breast pumps, and about 77 percent said they should receive prenatal care.

About 78 percent said that if immigration authorities separate a parent from an infant, they should be required to give the parent some contact with their baby.

How does this tie into the November elections?

Control of both the U.S. House and Senate are up for grabs in the November midterm elections, and it’s not clear yet how voters’ views on immigration policy and the Trump administration will affect their decisions.

Immigration is not currently a top issue for voters, but combined with Trump’s broader disapproval and weakened support for the GOP among Latinos — the group most affected by the administration’s immigration crackdown — the issue could still play an influential role in Florida, Texas, Arizona and beyond.

If Democrats win majorities in Congress, their party could exert greater oversight of the agencies carrying out Trump’s immigration agenda.

For example, Congress could revive a Biden-era rule that required DHS to report twice a year on how many pregnant, nursing or postpartum immigrants were held in immigration detention and include a “detailed justification” for every detained immigrant in these categories.

The 19th/YouGov poll was conducted online from September 18 to 24 among 2,357 adults, including an oversampling of 18- to 29-year-olds. The margin of error for the overall sample is ± 2.5 points.

title: NJ nonprofits sue Trump administration over housing counseling cuts • Jersey Vindicator
description:
New Jersey Citizen Action and the Housing and Community Development Network of New Jersey are among 10 organizations suing the Trump administration over the funding cuts.
The network and its participating agencies have received HUD counseling funds continuously since 2014.
New Jersey Citizen Action has provided housing counseling since 1993 and received HUD certification in 1995.
The HUD housing counseling funding supports about 9% of Citizen Action’s organizational budget, according to the lawsuit.
Defendants include Trump, HUD, HUD Secretary Scott Turner, the Office of Management and Budget, and its director, Russell Vought.
text:
The plaintiffs say the loss of federal funding threatens help for homebuyers, renters, and families facing foreclosure.

Two New Jersey nonprofits joined a federal lawsuit Tuesday challenging the Trump administration’s effort to cancel $56.1 million in housing counseling funding, warning that the cuts would undermine services that help residents buy homes, avoid foreclosure and remain housed.

New Jersey Citizen Action and the Housing and Community Development Network of New Jersey are among 10 organizations suing the Trump administration over the funding cuts. The complaint alleges the administration unlawfully withheld money Congress approved and targeted recipients because of their advocacy and political views.

The lawsuit, filed Sept. 29 in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, challenges the cancellation of nearly all of the $57.5 million Congress appropriated for HUD’s Comprehensive Housing Counseling program. It also contests new restrictions regarding which counseling services federal grants can cover.

The Housing and Community Development Network administers federal funding, training and compliance oversight for nine local HUD-approved counseling agencies serving most of New Jersey’s 21 counties, according to the complaint. The network and its participating agencies have received HUD counseling funds continuously since 2014. Its fiscal 2024-25 award totaled about $333,000.

New Jersey Citizen Action has provided housing counseling since 1993 and received HUD certification in 1995. Its free services include rental, foreclosure, financial, and homeownership counseling throughout all 21 counties, according to the complaint.

The HUD housing counseling funding supports about 9% of Citizen Action’s organizational budget, according to the lawsuit. The organization receives the money through the statewide network and says losing it would require reducing or reallocating its counseling capacity.

“NJ families and residents are in the midst of a housing affordability crisis, and will be deeply harmed by the White House rescission of HUD-housing counseling dollars,” Staci Berger, president and CEO of the Housing and Community Development Network of New Jersey, said in a statement about the lawsuit.

“We are pursuing this action to protect our neighbors and communities, so that they are able to access affordable, safe and stable housing using the wide array of HUD housing counseling services that Congress authorized,” Berger said.

Dena Mottola Jaborska, executive director of New Jersey Citizen Action, said the administration was targeting nonprofit providers and federal programs that offer a critical lifeline to people struggling with housing affordability.

The dispute centers on a maneuver the administration calls a “pocket rescission,” which involves proposing to cancel appropriated money shortly before the deadline to commit it, then withholding the funds as that deadline passes.

According to the complaint, President Donald Trump sent Congress the proposal Sept. 25, five days before the Sept. 30 deadline for HUD to commit the housing counseling funds. The organizations argue that the administration cannot cancel the money without Congress passing a law approving the rescission.

The White House defended the cuts in a Sept. 25 announcement, saying the counseling program had not demonstrated reduced mortgage delinquencies among counseled homebuyers, and accusing recipients of pursuing discriminatory diversity, equity, and inclusion agendas. It singled out the National Urban League and Housing Action Illinois, both plaintiffs in the lawsuit, criticizing their positions on immigration and racial justice.

The organizations cite those statements as evidence of unconstitutional retaliation. Their complaint alleges that the administration withheld funding to punish speech and advocacy outside the housing counseling program, violating the First Amendment. The lawsuit also argues that HUD violated federal spending requirements and the Administrative Procedure Act by abandoning longstanding policies without adequate explanation or consideration of organizations that relied on the funding.

Months of uncertainty preceded the funding dispute, according to the plaintiffs.

Federal housing officials did not release the fiscal 2025 funding notice until March 26, 2026, although the grant period was supposed to begin retroactively on Oct. 1, 2025. Applications were due May 26, and HUD listed Aug. 3 as the anticipated award date. In their complaint, the plaintiffs allege that the agency failed to make the funding available by that date.

While awaiting awards, counseling agencies continued serving clients and incurred expenses they expected federal grants to reimburse. The complaint says the delays forced organizations to draw down reserves, reduce services and defer spending, with some organizations laying off employees or withdrawing from the program.

The March funding notice also excluded one-on-one counseling for prospective homebuyers from eligible expenses, according to the complaint. It restricted federally funded counseling for existing homeowners to borrowers with mortgages made, insured, guaranteed, or held by HUD, the Department of Veterans Affairs, or the Department of Agriculture.

That change would prevent agencies from using grants for foreclosure-prevention counseling for borrowers with mortgages outside those categories, according to the organizations. They say HUD had funded those services for more than 30 years.

The plaintiffs are asking the court to order the administration to commit the appropriated funds and continue operating the counseling program. They also seek to preserve the money beyond the Sept. 30 deadline while the case proceeds and block enforcement of the challenged funding restrictions.

Besides the two New Jersey organizations, the plaintiffs include the National Urban League, Housing Action Illinois, North Carolina Housing Coalition, National CAPACD, Fair Housing Resource Center, Southwest Fresno Community Development Corporation, Somerville Community Corporation and the National Foundation for Debt Management.

Defendants include Trump, HUD, HUD Secretary Scott Turner, the Office of Management and Budget, and its director, Russell Vought.

text:

I am deeply concerned about your agreement with the LaSalle Family Foundation to allow an ICE detention facility to operate on land at the England Airpark for an ICE detention facility. Distressingly, I learned that this facility is being used to jail migrant children and families. Detaining children and families for immigration purposes is a human rights violation.

It is alarming to learn that the groundwater beneath England Airpark has a per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) concentration 575,000 times higher than the federal drinking water limit, making this site one of the most contaminated in the entirety of the United States of America. Further to my anguish is knowing that LaSalle Corrections, the parent company of the LaSalle Family Foundation, has a long history of abuse at their facilities throughout Louisiana. In October 2025, a jury awarded $42.75 million to the family of a man killed at a LaSalle correctional facility when guards slammed his head into a concrete floor. In January of 2024, in another facility run by LaSalle, officers indiscriminately pepper-sprayed an entire dorm of 200 people and cut off power and water to the entire unit as retaliation for a hunger strike. These are just two in a litany of violence that happen at these facilities.

I urge you to put a stop to the collaboration of England Airpark with ICE, cancel the contract with LaSalle Family Foundation, and close the detention facility operating in the airpark.

Yours sincerely,

description:
AUSTIN, Texas (CN) — A man shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent in Austin was moved into federal criminal detention on Wednesday, following a hearing in the criminal case against him.
Ten days after the shooting, Garces Perez has been held in immigration detention with a bullet still in his back.
During the hearing, Assistant U.S. Attorney Britni Verdeja reviewed the events that led prosecutors to criminally charge Garces Perez.
The footage showed Garces Perez’s car driving close to officer L.G., then officer D.F.
The court also saw security camera footage from a Bingo hall that showed the agents pursuing Garces Perez.
text:
AUSTIN, Texas (CN) — A man shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent in Austin was moved into federal criminal detention on Wednesday, following a hearing in the criminal case against him.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Dustin Howell found there was probable cause Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, a 28-year-old delivery driver from Venezuela, assaulted, resisted or impeded a federal officer during a Sept. 20 confrontation that ended with him being shot in the back.

In its criminal complaint, the government accuses Garces Perez of striking a federal officer, identified by his initials as L.G., with his driver-side mirror while fleeing from law enforcement. After hearing witness testimony from Homeland Security Investigations Special Agent Rick Bazan, the Department of Homeland Security’s lead investigator looking into the incident, and viewing footage of the confrontation, Howell granted the government’s motion to hold Garces Perez in federal criminal detention.

“I agree with the government that the charged crime is a crime of violence and that there is a risk that the defendant will flee,” Howell said at the end of the hearing.

Ten days after the shooting, Garces Perez has been held in immigration detention with a bullet still in his back. He entered the courtroom in Austin in a wheelchair with his arm in a sling.

During the hearing, Assistant U.S. Attorney Britni Verdeja reviewed the events that led prosecutors to criminally charge Garces Perez. Verdeja told the judge, “The reason he is in this predicament is because he decided to flee and strike an immigration officer.”

In an affidavit supporting the criminal charges, Bazan stated two federal agents, who are identified in the document by their initials, stopped Garces Perez and confronted him. During the interaction, one of the agents asked him to exit the vehicle, but Garces Perez ignored the command and asked to move his car into a parking lot, the affidavit claims.

“Approximately one minute later, Garces abruptly closed the window and drove off,” Bazan said. “L.G. tried to avoid contact with the car, but Garces’ driver’s side-view mirror struck L.G. in his torso as it drove off.”

Deja showed body camera footage of the interaction from one of the agents, identified as D.F. in court documents. The footage showed Garces Perez’s car driving close to officer L.G., then officer D.F. retreating to his vehicle to begin a chase. The court also saw security camera footage from a Bingo hall that showed the agents pursuing Garces Perez.

Federal Public Defender Shane McMahon, representing Garces Perez, asked Bazan if L.G. said he was assaulted when the car drove away. Bazan said he had not spoken to L.G. and only interviewed D.F. and Garces Perez following the incident.

In his closing argument, McMahon sought to cast doubt on whether the assault the government claims occurred ever happened.

“I saw the car drive away quickly, but I did not see the officer get struck,” McMahon said, referring to the video. “I think it is telling that even the officer has not claimed to have been struck.”

Verdeja, in support of her request to hold Garces Perez in detention, told the court: “There is no greater risk of flight than fleeing from officers, putting everyone else in our community in danger.”

As a result of Howell’s decision, Garces Perez will be held without bond while the investigation continues. If convicted, he faces up to 20 years in a federal prison.

Outside the courthouse, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, Garces Perez’s immigration attorney, told reporters her client’s immigration matters will continue while he remains in federal custody. Lincoln-Goldfinch also accused the government of using Section 111 of Title 18 of the United States Code, the law Garces Perez is accused of violating, to target anyone who protests, observes or opposes immigration agents.

“In 2025, the Department of Homeland Security sent federal prosecutors a record 274 referrals with Section 111 as the lead charge,” Lincoln-Goldfnich said. “It increasingly looks like a tool of retaliation against anyone who scrutinizes federal immigration enforcement.”

The lingering question that Garces Perez’s attorneys seemingly have no answer to is when or if he will receive medical attention to remove the bullet from his back. Lincoln-Goldfinch did not know when such a procedure might occur but said if the bullet was not removed soon, her client risks loss of mobility and sepsis.

text:
A private prison operator has signed a contract with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to reopen a shuttered Marana prison as an immigration detention center, with operations expected to begin within 60 days.

Management & Training Corp. said it signed the agreement on Tuesday. The company described the site as a 775-bed facility expected to employ about 338 full-time workers once it’s fully running.

MTC ran the prison for Arizona for nearly 30 years before the state closed it in late 2023.

U.S. Rep. Adelita Grijalva, who represents Marana, criticized the deal Wednesday. She raised concerns about how detainees would be cared for, the company’s track record and how many people the facility would hold.

The company said it would meet or go beyond ICE’s National Detention Standards and treat detainees with compassion.

“DHS is once again rushing to open another private detention facility over the objections of local residents,” Grijalva said in a statement.

In February, ICE posted a notice saying it planned to give MTC a two-year contract without seeking bids from other companies.

MTC would provide housing, guards, meals, medical care and transportation for detainees. The notice said the facility could hold up to 775 people, but a separate document laying out the facility details says it will house 513 detainees.

MTC’s announcement did not disclose the final contract’s value.

text:
A federal judge in California blocked federal agencies’ implementation of a $100,000 Trump administration charge for businesses to hire workers on H-1B visas.

In the aftermath of President Donald Trump’s proclamation establishing the fee for workers hired outside of the US, US Customs and Border Protection and US Citizenship and Immigration Services issued memoranda and guidance on frequently asked questions pertaining to entry and exit from the US, how to pay the fee, and other details.

Those agencies are enjoined from enforcing or implementing policies under the proclamation as well as an extension issued by the White House this month until notice-and-comment rulemaking under the Administrative Procedure Act takes place, Judge Haywood S. Gilliam Jr said in an order Wednesday.

It’s the second district court ruling against the proclamation that upended hiring through the specialty occupation visa program. A federal judge in Boston found the policy unlawful in June and an appellate court later denied the administration’s request to stay that decision, meaning the fee has been blocked for the past two months.

Haywood denied a request to grant class certification to employers affected by the $100,000 charge, finding it was unnecessary.

The lawsuit is one of multiple legal challenges to the fee, issued last year through a White House proclamation that was the administration’s most restrictive measure so far on hiring of high-skilled workers.

Another challenge to the fee led by the US Chamber of Commerce is pending before the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. A US District Court for the District of Columbia judge last year denied an injunction on the $100,000 fee sought by the Chamber.

The fee didn’t apply to workers approved for H-1B status within the US like recent college graduates. But it effectively blocked most international hiring for employers like hospitals, research universities, churches, and K-12 schools.

The Trump administration cited legal authority under the Immigration and Nationality Act that gives the president broad power to restrict entry to the US. But plaintiffs led by California-based nurse recruiting firm argued that the statute doesn’t allow the president to upend visa programs and fee regimes designed by lawmakers. And a Supreme Court ruling overturning President Trump’s global tariffs bolstered that case by finding only Congress has tax authority, they argued.

Wednesday’s decision protects a system thrown into chaos by the proclamation and reaffirms that no president can “rewrite immigration policy with the stroke of a pen,” said Steve Bressler, a senior legal advisor at Democracy Forward, which represents plaintiffs.

“Communities across this country depend on skilled professionals who care for patients, teach students, build infrastructure, conduct research, and serve congregations,” he said in a statement. “The administration tried to financially punish companies with an arbitrary, unauthorized, and deeply harmful $100,000 fee imposed without Congress.“

Plaintiffs are also represented by Justice Action Center, Cohen Milstein Sellers & Toll PLLC, Kuck Baxter Immigration, LLC, Bless Litigation, and the South Asian American Justice Collaborative. The government is represented by the Department of Justice.

description:
BALTIMORE — Concerns are growing about overcrowding issues at Baltimore's immigration facility as the U.S. Supreme Court allows third-country deportations to resume.
Baltimore ICE facility faces overcrowding allegations despite judge's order Separately, Baltimore's immigration detention facility faces allegations of overcrowding and poor conditions.

text:
BALTIMORE —

Concerns are growing about overcrowding issues at Baltimore's immigration facility as the U.S. Supreme Court allows third-country deportations to resume.

A U.S. Supreme Court order issued Tuesday halts an appeals court ruling and allows the Trump administration to continue third-country deportations, a policy that allows U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to send undocumented migrants to countries to which they have no connection.

Last week, the Trump administration canceled a flight carrying 70 people to three different countries after a federal court ruled migrants should have the opportunity to contest such deportations.

"People who are currently in detention, or maybe aren't even in detention right now, but have been granted withholding of removal or relief under the Convention Against Torture, they are at serious risk of being deported to a country that they have never been to," said Briana Arnold, an immigration partner attorney at Killian Law Group.

Immigration attorney raises risks

Arnold explained that migrants could face significant risks if deported.

"The two main issues are, No. 1, that these detainees are being persecuted or even tortured in these third countries. And, No. 2, a lot of them are being sent to the country that the United States granted them protection from," Arnold told WBAL-TV 11 News Investigates.

She also raised concerns about the lack of due process for migrants.

"They are at serious risk of being deported to a country that they have never been to."

"The United States is really just throwing up their hands and saying, 'Once you are there, you are their responsibility.' And, in many cases, it violates a lot of their rights," Arnold told WBAL-TV 11 News Investigates.

The Supreme Court's order allowing third-country deportations is not final, as the high court is expected to hear arguments on the policy in December to determine its legality.

Baltimore ICE facility faces overcrowding allegations despite judge's order

Separately, Baltimore's immigration detention facility faces allegations of overcrowding and poor conditions. U.S. District Judge Julie Rubin has cited Baltimore's ICE facility for failing to comply with her March ruling addressing overcrowding and health concerns.

"In these tiny cells, they'd pack up to 50 or 60 people where there was no room to even sit, much less lay down — even if people were there for several days,” said Amelia Dagen, senior attorney at the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights.

Rubin's March order required a minimum of 31 square feet of space per person, access to medication and routine medical screenings.

Dagen told WBAL-TV 11 News Investigates that the Baltimore facility was not providing access to medications, showers or toothbrushes, and that cells and bathrooms were not being cleaned.

"We're seeing very many days that were higher ... sometimes over 70 people."

"Pretty quickly after the March order, we started hearing from people who were at the Baltimore holding room that this wasn't happening," Dagen told WBAL-TV 11 News Investigates. "It was inconsistent at best."

A WBAL-TV 11 News Investigates review of ICE data collected after the order revealed that the Baltimore facility was overcrowded 60% of the time.

"The total facility population is 45 people, and, unfortunately, we're seeing very many days that were higher than that, sometimes over 70 people," Dagen told WBAL-TV 11 News Investigates.

Rubin is now requiring the Baltimore ICE field office to file a report every two weeks to ensure compliance with her March order.

Also in March, Maryland's attorney general filed a federal lawsuit in an effort to obtain records detailing conditions at Baltimore's ICE facility. In September, the government denied the allegations of overcrowding.

ICE has not responded to requests from WBAL-TV 11 News Investigates for comment.

text:
PONCE, Puerto Rico —The US Department of Homeland Security inaugurated today a new joint facility during a ribbon-cutting ceremony marking a major investment in CBP and Coast Guard operations and mission readiness in southern Puerto Rico.

The new DHS joint facility, in the Port of Ponce, will house US Coast Guard Resident Inspection Office Ponce and the U.S. Customs and Border Protection Air and Marine Operations Ponce Marine Unit.

These units support CBP and Coast Guard personnel responsible for maritime safety and prevention, border security, inspections and law enforcement operations in the region.

“The Ponce Marine Unit plays a critical role in detecting, interdicting and responding to maritime threats across Puerto Rico’s southern approaches,” said Christopher Hunter, Director of the Caribbean Air and Marine Branch. “This new facility gives our agents the modern operational, maintenance and coordination space they need to work seamlessly with Coast Guard and local partners, strengthen border security, and protect the people and commerce that depend on a secure Caribbean maritime domain.”

The nearly $22 million project included demolition of the former facility, construction of a new two-story, 9,650-square-foot complex with dedicated office, training, operational, security and maintenance spaces. Additionally, the site features a 1,880-square-foot boat maintenance bay, improved pier and boat ramp infrastructure, upgraded utilities, parking, and emergency backup power.

The award, design and construction of this turn-key project was accomplished in partnership with CBP, AMO, USCG, the Coast Guard’s Facilities Design and Construction Center, the CBP Office of Facilities and Asset Management.

"This project is a tangible, long-term investment that reinforces Department of Homeland Security operational readiness and critical infrastructure protection across the Caribbean,” said Capt. Luis J. Rodriguez, Commander of U.S. Coast Guard Sector San Juan. “Our Coast Guard and CBP teams in this new facility can operate, communicate and coordinate faster and more effectively with local law enforcement and port partners strengthening our collective capability to secure waterways, support vital commerce, and safeguard the Caribbean maritime domain."

The DHS joint facility is immediately next to the United States Custom House in Ponce, the oldest existing customhouse in Puerto Rico. Built in 1841, this adobe building of the Spanish era is historically and architecturally significant and is listed on the U.S. National Register of Historic Places.

Expanding this regional maritime footprint, the U.S. Coast Guard assumed control of historic regional lighthouses near Ponce in 1933, including the Cardona Island and Caja de Muertos Lights while the Port of Ponce itself served as a vital logistics hub during World War II.

Today, DHS, CBP, and the Coast Guard work together to secure the nation’s borders, safeguard maritime commerce, and support public safety throughout Puerto Rico and the surrounding region.
